Finally, one study [ 28 ] adopted the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines for the management of severe sepsis and septic shock. Interventions favoring macrolides The studies reviewed various interventions that assessed the anti-inflammatory effects of macrolides on patient outcomes with CAP (see Additional file 4 for characteristics of included studies). Macrolide-containing regimens frequently showed favorable outcomes, especially among patients with specific risk factors or severe illness. In a prospective longitudinal study by Lorenzo et al. (2015) [ 29 ] involving 52 patients with poor responses after 72 h of antibiotic treatment, β-lactam/macrolide (BLM) therapy was linked to a shorter hospitalization compared to those not receiving macrolides. Similarly, Stahl et al. (1999) [ 32 ] reported that the hospital stay was reduced to 2.8 days in patients receiving macrolides ( n = 12) within the 24 h of admission at the New England Medical Center, compared to 5.3 days for those not receiving macrolides ( n = 64). Three prospective observational studies investigated macrolide use in CAP. Tessmer et al. (2009) [ 30 ] found that 51% of 1844 patients with CAP received BLM therapy. Martin-Loeches et al. (2010) [ 11 ] reported that 175 out of 218 patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation due to CAP received a macrolide-containing regimen across 27 ICUs in 9 countries. Ceccato et al. (2019) [ 15 ] revealed that 932 out of 1715 patients admitted to the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona between 1996 and 2016 received BLM therapy. These studies consistently found that the combination of β-lactam and macrolide was associated with lower mortality rates, particularly in patients with higher CRB56 risk classes [ 30 ] and severe inflammatory responses [ 11 ]. A prospective observational multicenter study by Periera et al. (2018) [ 26 ] reported that 502 patients were admitted across 14 Portuguese hospitals within 1 year, and 76% received combination therapy—primary β-lactam and macrolide (80%). The combination was linked to both a reduced length of stay and a lower 6-month mortality rate. Another prospective observational study by Aspa et al. (2006) [ 27 ] analyzed 638 patients from 35 Spanish hospitals, divided into treatment groups: β-lactam monotherapy ( n = 251), macrolide monotherapy ( n = 37), β-lactam plus macrolide ( n = 198), levofloxacin alone/combination ( n = 48), and other combinations ( n = 104). The results indicated that the initial antibiotic regimen independently influenced the 30-day mortality rate, especially among patients with a high pneumonia severity index. In Arnold et al. (2016) [ 17 ], a prospective study involving 40 participants found that only 14 received macrolides while the others did not. This study, the first to evaluate the effect of macrolides on innate immunity, reported no fatalities, with a 2-day shorter length of stay and a half-day faster clinical stabilization in the macrolide group. Levels of certain cytokines (IL-6, IL-8) also approached significantly lower levels in the macrolide group. Finally, a double-blind, randomized, multicenter trial by Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al. (2008) [ 28 ] assessed the impact of clarithromycin in patients with sepsis and VAP. Among 100 patients receiving clarithromycin between June 2004 and November 2005 in Greek hospitals, the length of hospital stay and mortality were significantly lower than in the placebo group ( n = 100). These results suggest that clarithromycin has a positive impact on patient outcomes. Interventions not favoring macrolides In hospitalized adults, the addition of a macrolide to treatment did not yield additional clinical advantages. Loh et al. (2005) [ 31 ] conducted an observational study involving prospective patients admitted to an urban-based hospital in Malaysia across two recruitment periods, from March 2003 to July 2004. Macrolide treatment began on the first day of admission. After 16 months, data from 141 patients (of the 226 initially recruited) were analyzed; 45% received a macrolide and 55% received a single broad-spectrum antibiotic. The study found that adding macrolides to broad-spectrum antibiotics did not provide any additional clinical benefit for patients with either severe or no severe pneumonia. No differences were observed in mortality rate, length of hospital stay, or the need for intubation and assisted ventilation. Paul et al. (2007) [ 34 ] conducted the TREAT trial across three teaching-based institutions in three countries. The study enrolled 611 patients, of whom 74% received a β-lactam, while 26% received empirical antibiotic treatment with an added macrolide. The 30-day mortality rate was 7% in the combination therapy group versus 22% in the β-lactam group. However, the mean length of hospital stay was comparable between the two groups. The authors noted significant differences between the two patient groups that may not be fully captured, suggesting variations in patient characteristics that could have influenced mortality outcomes. In a prospective clinical trial, Yadegarynia et al. (2022) [ 33 ] recruited patients from a hospital in Tehran and randomly assigned them to two treatment groups. Participants were matched for gender, age, and sex. The first group received azithromycin and ceftriaxone, while the second group received levofloxacin. The study concluded that hospitalized CAP patients may benefit more from fluoroquinolone treatment than from the combination of β-lactam and macrolide, although no significant difference in mortality was observed between the two treatment groups. Finally, Greco Kinney et al. (2023) [ 35 ] conducted a prospective observational cohort study from March 2020 to July 2022. The study involving 149 patients with severe CAP was admitted to the medical ICU (MICU) of an academic quaternary medical center in the USA, where 63 patients received azithromycin as treatment and 86 patients received doxycycline. As results, no statistically significant difference in mortality rate or length of hospital stay was found between patients treated with β-lactams plus doxycycline versus azithromycin. Excluded studies Twenty-three studies were excluded from the review. The reasons for exclusion are summarized in the Additional file 5 (See additional file 5 for reasons for the excluded studies). Risk of bias in included studies The review assessed the quality of the thirteen studies. Three of them were found to have randomized controlled trial (RCT) designs [ 28 , 33 , 34 ]. The quality of evidence of these studies was individually evaluated using the Cochrane tool for risk of bias. Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al. (2008) [ 28 ] scored “low risk” in the domains related to selection bias, performance bias which included blinding of participants and personnel, attrition bias, reporting bias, and other risks of bias. In addition, the risk of bias was unclear about detection bias. As for Paul et al. (2007) [ 34 ], it scored “low risk” in the domains related to attrition bias, performance bias which included blinding of participants and personnel, reporting bias, and other risks of bias. In addition, the risk of bias was unclear about selection bias, and detection bias. Yadegarynia et al. (2022) [ 33 ] scored “low risk” in the domain related to selection bias (Random Sequence Generation), attrition bias, reporting bias, and other risks of bias. It scored high in the domain related to performance bias, which included blinding of participants and personnel. In addition, the risk of bias was unclear about selection bias (Allocation Concealment), and detection bias. Upon applying the MINORS methodological index for grading the nine included non-comparative articles, the resulting scores ranged from 17/24 to 23/24 for the eight domains included in the adopted tool for non-comparative studies. The mean and median scores were 19.9 and 20, respectively. Four studies [ 11 , 15 , 26 , 35 ] had a MINORS score of 21/24 or higher and were considered to have a low risk of bias while the other studies’ scores ranged from 17/24 to 20/24 and were reported with moderate risk of bias. In brief, all studies assessed with MINORS had clearly stated the aim, inclusion of consecutive patients, and prospective collection of data. Quality assessment was conducted independently by two reviewers (AA and RN) and achieved a uniform bias assessment. Detailed risk of bias assessment using MINORS for included studies in this review is presented in Additional file 6 for Summary of Risk of Bias-MINORS. Effects of admission of macrolides Results were pooled separately for RCTs and non-RCTs to ensure the robustness of the findings. This separation is essential because, in contrast to RCTs, non-randomized research could bring different biases. A meta-analysis for randomized controlled trials (RCT) [ 28 , 33 , 34 ] was not possible in this review due to differences in interventions, patients’ populations, and outcomes; the study’s findings are instead summarized narratively. This approach guarantees that the findings are still included in the review while preventing the inclusion of biases that could occur from trying to combine data from a single study. In addition, the control group in the selected studies comprised patients receiving treatment with non-macrolide alternative antibiotics. According to the treatment guidelines, these therapies specifically included fluoroquinolones, beta-lactam monotherapy, and additional medications including doxycycline. Studies were included if they offered a clear comparison between the macrolide-treated intervention group and the control group receiving any of these other therapies were included in the analysis. This specificity was necessary to evaluate the changes in treatment regimens and their potential impact on results across the studies. Mortality rate during hospitalization Mortality NRS (acute up to 7 days or during hospitalization) A meta-analysis of five studies [ 11 , 17 , 26 , 31 , 32 ] involving 738 patients, compared clinical outcomes—specifically, the mortality rate between two patient groups: one receiving the standard regimen and the other receiving a combination of antibiotics, including a macrolide. As shown in Fig. 2 , the administration of a macrolide had a statistically significant impact (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.71) indicating that adding a macrolide could reduce the mortality rate within the first 7 days of hospitalization. The I2 value of 18% suggests that only a low percentage of the variation in effect sizes across studies was due to heterogeneity, meaning most variation could be attributed to sampling error (chance). However, the certainty of evidence supporting macrolide administration was low, due to the observational study design and the high risk of bias in most individual studies. The analysis showed a statistically significant effect (mean difference − 0.68, 95% CI − 1.67 to 0.32), indicating that administering may reduce the length of hospital stay. The I2 value of 20% suggests that only a small portion of the variability in effect estimates was due to heterogeneity, with most of the variability attributed to sampling error (chance) (Fig. 4 ). However, the certainty of the evidence supporting macrolide administration was relatively low, as most individual studies were observational and carried a high risk of bias. Fig. 4 Effect of macrolide therapy on length of hospital stay in patients with CAP ( N = 6) Other outcomes In a prospective observational study by Lorenzo et al. (2015) [ 29 ], the cytokine profiles, particularly tumor necrosis factors (TNF), were analyzed as clinical outcomes in patients with CAP. Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most frequent etiological micro-organism identified in CAP cases. The results showed that IL-6 and TNF-α levels in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), as well as the level of IL-8 in blood, were lower in patients treated with a macrolide regimen. However, there were no significant differences in overall blood cytokine levels between patients treated with a macrolide and those who were not. Another prospective study by Arnold et al. (2016) [ 17 ] assessed the neutrophil function and cytokine and chemokine levels. Although no statistically significant differences were found between the treatment groups for most cytokine levels, the levels of IL-6, IL-8, and 12p40 were lower in the macrolide group. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the available data regarding the use of macrolides as immunomodulators in the treatment of CAP and VAP and to evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention on several outcomes, including mortality rate, length of stay, recurrence of pneumonia within 90 days, and clinical stability. In nine out of the 13 studies, the use of macrolides as anti-inflammatory agents in the treatment of CAP and VAP was found to be effective in reducing mortality rate and length of stay as primary outcomes among adult patients, compared to standard treatment. The meta-analyses of included studies confirmed these findings, showing a consistent reduction in mortality rates during hospitalization when patients received a β-lactam and macrolide combination, compared with monotherapy or fluoroquinolone + β-lactam combination. The pooled OR of 0.42 (95% CI 0.25–0.71) indicates that patients receiving macrolides were 58% less likely to die during hospitalization than those who did not ( p = 0.001). The low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 18%) suggests that the effect of macrolides on mortality is generally consistent across studies and patient demographics. These findings aligned with the results of Asadi et al. (2012) [ 36 ], which reported that macrolide use was associated with a 22% decrease in mortality in hospitalized CAP patients compared to non-macrolide regimens. The reduction highlighted suggests that the use of macrolides in the treatment of patients with CAP decreases the likelihood of death during hospitalization compared with those who received standard treatment. This effect is mostly noticeable in the study by Periera et al. (2018) [ 26 ], which had the largest sample size and highest weight in the analysis. However, no significant difference was found in multiple individual studies [ 31 , 32 ], highlighting inconsistencies in the results. In particular, Arnold et al. (2016) [ 17 ] had a relatively small sample size (40 patients) and a very low incidence rate (0 events in the macrolide group). Due to the observational nature of the study, selection bias may exist, and the estimated uncertainty is reflected by the large confidence interval (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.81). Moreover, the small sample size in the study by Stahl et al. (1999) [ 32 ] (76 patients) reduces the ability to detect differences among groups. With a non-significant result (OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.11 to 30.74) and a very wide confidence interval, the study's findings indicate that small sample size has a significant influence, raising uncertainty and decreasing reliability [ 32 ]. In the post-discharge period, the meta-analysis results showed that patients treated with macrolides were 48% less likely to die within 30 days post-discharge compared to those who did not receive macrolides (pooled OR of 0.52, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.25–0.71). However, the moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 65%) suggests variation in the effect of macrolides on mortality reduction across different trials and patient populations. This suggests that post-discharge mortality may significantly decrease with the use of macrolides, offering a sustained protective impact that could help stabilize patients as they transition back to outpatient care. This effect, most pronounced in the studies by Paul et al. (2007) [ 34 ] and Tessmer et al. (2009) [ 30 ], shows a statistically significant decrease in the mortality rate. This finding is particularly significant as it demonstrates how macrolides might improve long-term outcomes and lower readmission rates. When comparing our study’s findings to those of other studies, the main problem is that no observational study has shown that combined therapy is beneficial in lowering 30-day mortality. Moreover, Baddour et al. (2004) [ 37 ] confirmed that combination therapy including macrolides was associated with lower 14-day mortality among critically ill patients. The results of the meta-analysis examining the effect of macrolides on the length of hospital stay indicate a potential effect of macrolide administration, but this effect is not statistically significant. The strongest evidence comes from the study by Lorenzo et al. (2015) [ 29 ], which shows a significant reduction in hospital length of stay. Although this finding is statistically insignificant, the overall pooled mean difference of − 0.68 indicates a trend towards a shorter length of stay for patients receiving macrolides. The low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 20%) suggests consistency across studies, but further research is needed to confirm these findings. No meta-analysis was found in the literature search to support or compare these findings. The clinical benefits observed with the use of macrolides in the management of CAP can be related to several factors. Macrolides are used mainly for their antimicrobial effects, but their immunomodulating effects could also be related to the clinical benefits, which include the prevention of complications like acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and sepsis, which are major causes of death in hospitalized patients [ 1 , 38 ]. This is particularly relevant in pneumococcal CAP and in patients with a high level of inflammation, i.e., CRP levels higher than 15 mg/dL, as shown in the study by Baddour et al. (2004) [ 37 ]. Furthermore, macrolides are active against a wide range of pathogens, including atypical bacteria, not always covered by conventional antibiotics, and may be helpful in the management of co-infection and secondary infection, hence reducing the risk of mortality [ 39 ]. Therefore, the observed associations between macrolide use and improved outcomes should be interpreted in the context of both their antimicrobial effects and potential immunomodulatory properties, without inferring direct causality. Moreover, the timing of macrolide administration appears crucial. In patients with severe CAP, Periera et al. (2018) [ 26 ] found that the macrolide intervention significantly improved both 6-month and in-hospital mortality rates, especially in patients who received treatment within the first 6 h after diagnosis. Moreover, Stahl et al. (1999) [ 32 ] reported that the hospital length of stay was shorter for patients receiving macrolides within 24 h of admission compared with those not receiving macrolides. Administering a macrolide early during hospital admission could ensure that anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects occur at a critical point in the patient’s illness trajectory, preventing further complications [ 40 ]. To improve patient outcomes, future research should focus on determining the optimal time for macrolide administration. However, it is important to highlight the limitations of the study. First, the majority of the included studies were observational, which limits the ability to control for confounders such as age, underlying health conditions, and concurrent treatment, in addition to unmeasured confounding that could still arise despite the use of multivariable analyses. Second, there is a low level of certainty in the evidence across the included studies, mainly because many of the individual studies encompassed in the analysis had a significant risk of bias, mostly caused by observational study designs. Third, language bias may also be present as only English-language publications were included which potentially excludes other relevant studies published in different languages. Fourth, the variability in the types of macrolides used in the treatment of CAP, including azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin, affects their effectiveness in reducing mortality and hospital length of stay due to the unique pharmacokinetics and spectrum of activity of each [ 41 ]. Furthermore, the variety of macrolide dosages used, the inconsistency in the duration of therapy, the different times of administration, and the combination with other antibiotics reported can affect the mortality rate and hospital length of stay as primary outcomes in this study. Additionally, the presence of macrolide-resistant pathogens, as reported in some included studies, may influence treatment effectiveness and clinical outcomes, thereby introducing further variability in the observed results. Furthermore, Publication bias could not be formally assessed due to the limited number of included studies (< 10 per meta-analysis), which may affect the robustness of the findings. Finally, the small sample sizes in some studies may not adequately represent the larger population and could influence the generalizability of findings. These results emphasize the need for larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials to support these findings and better understand the efficacy of macrolide usage in clinical practice. Future research should also aim to better distinguish between the antimicrobial and potential immunomodulatory effects of macrolides, particularly in well-defined patient subgroups. Conclusions Findings from this systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that adding macrolides to standard antibiotic regimens for CAP and VAP may reduce in-hospital and post-discharge mortality, as well as hospital length of stay. However, several limitations, including the observational nature of the study designs, small sample sizes, variations in the types of macrolides used, and a high risk of bias, highlight the need for more reliable randomized controlled trials to confirm our findings. documents.title: Effect of targeted therapies on pulmonary function in rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a serious extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) associated with increased morbidity and mortality. The pulmonary safety of biologic Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs (bDMARDs) and targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) in RA-associated ILD (RA-ILD) remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the effect of bDMARDs and tsDMARDs on ILD progression in RA, focusing on pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters-forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO)-and, when available, high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed and Cochrane databases were searched up to 2025 for controlled trials and observational studies, including patients with RA fulfilling the 1987 ACR or 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria. Studies reporting longitudinal changes in PFTs or HRCT after bDMARD or tsDMARD treatment were included. Meta-analyses were conducted using the inverse variance method (RevMan V.5.4.1) for pooled estimates of FVC and DLCO.
RESULTS: 18 observational studies including 958 patients (mean age 65 years; 57% female) were analysed. The most frequent ILD patterns were usual interstitial pneumonia (48%) and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (40%). Data were available for rituximab (six studies), abatacept (4), JAK inhibitors (4), tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors (1) and tocilizumab (1). Pooled analysis showed no significant overall change in FVC (mean difference -0.85%, 95% CI -2.40 to 0.71; p=0.29) or DLCO (+0.79, 95% CI -0.30 to 1.88; p=0.16).
CONCLUSION: bDMARDs and tsDMARDs appear to stabilise pulmonary function in RA-ILD, without significant differences between agents. Further prospective studies integrating PFT and HRCT endpoints are needed to better define their pulmonary safety and long-term effects.
documents.conclusions: bDMARDs and tsDMARDs appear to stabilise pulmonary function in RA-ILD, without significant differences between agents. Further prospective studies integrating PFT and HRCT endpoints are needed to better define their pulmonary safety and long-term effects.

Overall, targeted therapies were associated with stabilisation of lung function, with consistent trends toward preservation of FVC and DLCO observed with JAK inhibitors. Rituximab was associated with an improvement in DLCO among patients with more severe baseline pulmonary impairment. This work helps inform therapeutic decision-making in the absence of randomised trials and highlights the need for prospective studies specifically designed for RA-ILD populations. Introduction Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease primarily characterised by synovial inflammation and progressive joint damage, with a global prevalence from 0.25% to 1%. 1 It can occur at any age, but women are affected two to three times more frequently than men. Extra-articular involvement is common in RA. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is one of the most severe complications, affecting about 6% of patients with RA. 2 RA-associated ILD (RA-ILD) is increasingly recognised as a leading cause of morbidity and premature mortality in patients with RA. 1 3 Median survival in patients with RA-ILD has been reported to range between 2 and 14 years. 4 Recent studies indicate that respiratory function parameters, particularly FVC and DLCO, tend to decline in the absence of treatment. 5 Its pathogenesis remains only partially understood and involves a complex interplay between systemic autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodelling of the lung. Established risk factors for RA-ILD include older age, male sex, smoking history, severe articular disease, high titres rheumatoid factor (RF) and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides (ACPA). 6 RA-ILD is heterogeneous, with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) being the most frequent radiological pattern, associated with a poorer prognosis compared with non-UIP forms. 7 Over the last two decades, biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (tsDMARDs) have transformed the therapeutic landscape of RA by targeting specific immune pathways to improve disease control and prevent structural joint damage. 8 9 However, their efficacy in RA-associated ILD remains poorly characterised. No randomised clinical trials have specifically addressed this population, and available evidence is largely limited to observational studies, case series or post-hoc analyses, leaving significant uncertainty in guiding treatment decisions. 6 Nevertheless, this aspect is increasingly acknowledged in recent guidelines, underlining the need for robust data to guide therapeutic strategies. 10 Existing data suggest that bDMARDs may slow the progression of RA-ILD. 11 More recently, new studies have evaluated the efficacy of JAK inhibitors (JAKi) in RA-ILD, suggesting potential benefit. 12 This uncertainty poses a major clinical challenge, as the optimal management of RA-ILD remains undefined. Given the rarity of this complication and the limited evidence, conducting randomised clinical trials in this population is currently impractical. Together, these gaps highlight the need for a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence on the efficacy of b/tsDMARDs in RA-ILD. The present meta-analysis therefore aims to synthesise available data on the efficacy of biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs in patients with RA and interstitial lung involvement, providing a clearer understanding of their potential benefits and risks and supporting informed clinical decision-making in this high-risk population. Methods Search strategy This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) to identify studies published until 2025. In addition, abstracts presented at the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) annual congresses from 2022 to 2024 were screened. The search strategy included the following terms: PubMed: (‘interstitial lung disease’ AND ‘Arthritis, Rheumatoid’(Mesh)) AND ‘Arthritis, Rheumatoid/therapy’(Mesh) Cochrane CENTRAL: ‘rheumatoid arthritis and interstitial lung disease’ We limited the search to articles written in English and reporting on randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies involving adults (age>18 years). In addition, we manually searched the reference lists of all included studies to identify any additional eligible reports. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by three reviewers (VB, EV and SH), followed by full-text assessment for eligibility. Duplicate references were removed prior to screening. The review protocol was registered in the international prospective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO; ID: 1178039). Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they met all of the following criteria: Study design: randomised controlled trials or observational cohort studies. Population: adult patients with RA fulfilling the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (studies relying solely on the 1987 criteria were excluded). Intervention: biologic DMARDs (including tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, anti-CD20 agents or abatacept) or targeted synthetic DMARDs (JAKi). Outcomes: pulmonary outcomes, including PFT parameter (CVF, DLCO, 6-min walk test) and HRCT parameters, assessed between 6 and 18 months of follow-up. Antifibrotic treatments were not considered in this meta-analysis. Data extraction Data were extracted independently by three reviewers (EV, VB and SH) using a standardised data collection form. The following information was retrieved: Study characteristics (design, sample size and duration) Baseline patient characteristics (age, sex, RA duration and fulfilment of classification criteria) Disease activity measures (eg, DAS28-CRP) Pulmonary parameters: HRCT pattern, pulmonary function tests (forced vital capacity (FVC), diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO), total lung capacity (TLC) and 6-min walking distance) Safety outcomes (infections and drug intolerance). Data reported as median and IQR were converted to mean and SD using the method described by Wan et al . 13 Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias in non-randomised studies was assessed using the ROBINS-E (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Exposures) tool. RCTs were evaluated using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2.0) ( online supplemental figure 1 ). Statistical analysis We conducted the meta-analysis in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Forced vital capacity (FVC), diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) and 6-min walk test were analysed as continuous variables. For each outcome, pooled mean differences (MDs) and corresponding 95% CIs were calculated using the inverse-variance method within a random-effects model to account for potential heterogeneity across studies. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the χ² test and quantified with the I² statistic. A random-effects model was applied in the presence of substantial heterogeneity (I² >50%). Sensitivity analyses were performed, including analyses restricted to patients with baseline FVC <80%, studies with a median follow-up of 12 months and studies enrolling more than 20 patients. Publication bias was assessed visually by inspection of funnel plot symmetry, generated using RevMan V.5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration) ( online supplemental figure 2 ). All analyses were conducted using Review Manager (RevMan) V.5.3 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, Copenhagen). For outcomes that could not be meta-analysed— HRCT pattern and evolution—a narrative synthesis was provided. Results A total of 874 records were initially identified. After removal of duplicates, 803 records were screened by title and abstract, and 21 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Three studies were excluded due to insufficient data 14 16 , leaving 18 studies 1217 33 that met the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis. The study selection process is shown in figure 1 . Figure 1 Flow Chart of the study. The 18 included studies comprised 984 patients with RA-ILD. The mean age was 64.9 years, 56.7% were women, and the mean RA disease duration was 115 months. The mean follow-up time after treatment initiation was 12 months (11/18 studies) and beyond 18 months (5/18 studies). Baseline data corresponded to the time of treatment initiation. Regarding ILD patterns, UIP accounted for 46.1% of cases and NSIP for 37.8%, while other patterns, such as organising pneumonia or mixed forms, were less frequent. In terms of therapeutic exposure, six cohorts evaluated rituximab, 2123 25 28 29 31 32 four abatacept, 17 18 22 27 four JAKi, 12 19 27 30 33 one TNF inhibitor 20 and one tocilizumab. 26 Concomitant use of csDMARDs and glucocorticoids was variably reported but was not considered in the meta-analysis because of data heterogeneity ( online supplemental table 1 ). At baseline, FVC data were available for 1144 patients and DLCO data for 1131 patients. Missing data during follow-up were minimal ( figures1 2 ). Risk of bias and quality assessment All included studies were observational, most of them with a retrospective design. However, according to the ROBINS-E tool, all studies were judged to be at low risk of bias, reflecting minor concerns in design and reporting limitations ( table 1 and online supplemental table 1 ). No randomised controlled trials specifically addressing the treatment of RA-ILD were identified. Forced vital capacity FVC data were available across the 18 studies included in the meta-analysis, comprising 984 patients at baseline and 973 at the end of follow-up ( figure 2 ). When pooling all treatments, no significant difference in FVC change was observed (mean difference −0.79, 95% CI −2.18 to 0.6, p=0.27). A significant decline in FVC was noted among patients treated with abatacept (mean difference −1.80, 95% CI −3.56 to −0.05, p=0.04). Although rituximab appeared to exert a relevant effect, it did not achieve a statistically significant improvement (mean difference +2.98, 95% CI −1.66 to 7.56, p=0.21). A substantial number of studies on JAK inhibitors indicated stable FVC values (mean difference +0.20, 95% CI −3.57 to 3.96, p=0.92). Other agents generally stabilised FVC, although the available data remain insufficient to draw firm conclusions regarding TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab. Only two studies assessed FVC progression according to the chest CT ILD patterns in patients treated with rituximab. 21 24 However, the available data remain inconsistent. In the small cohort reported by Duarte et al (n=3 UIP cases), no significant change in FVC was observed over time. 21 Conversely, Narváez et al found a significant improvement in FVC among patients with a UIP pattern (73.1±16.4% vs 79.2±20.3% at 12 months, p=0.004; p<0.001 at 24 months), which was similarly observed in patients with non-UIP patterns. 24 In an additional analysis of the abatacept cohort reported by Fernández-Díaz et al , 22 Atienza-Mateo et al 17 examined FVC progression according to the Chest CT ILD patterns. FVC values showed no significant change over 24 months in either UIP (82.1±21.4% vs 81.0±15.0%) or NSIP subgroups, supporting a stabilising effect of abatacept on pulmonary function irrespective of the underlying radiological pattern DLCO DLCO data were available from the 18 studies included in the meta-analysis, encompassing 984 patients at baseline and 973 at the end of follow-up ( figure 3 ). When all treatments were pooled, no significant overall change in DLCO was observed (mean difference +1.81, 95% CI −0.44 to 4.05, p=0.12). Treatment-specific analyses showed that no agent significantly modified DLCO progression. Rituximab exhibited the most consistent trend toward improvement, with a mean increase of +3.46% (95% CI −0.70 to 7.61, p=0.10). Abatacept appeared to maintain stable DLCO values over time (mean difference +0.81%, 95% CI −1.86 to 3.46, p=0.55). JAKi similarly demonstrated stability (mean difference +2.13%, 95% CI −4.02 to 8.28, p=0.50), while data for TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab, although limited, were consistent with a comparable preservation of pulmonary function. Regarding DLCO evolution according to Chest CT ILD patterns, data for rituximab are inconsistent. One study, conducted in a very small number of patients, did not report any significant change. 21 Another study observed an increase in DLCO at 12 and 24 months, but only in patients with a UIP pattern. 24 In the study evaluating abatacept, no significant change in DLCO was observed in patients with a UIP pattern. In contrast, patients with an NSIP pattern showed a significant increase in DLCO at 24 months. 17 6-minutes walk test The 6 min walk test (6MWT), reported longitudinally in three studies assessing rituximab or JAKi, 19 showed a non-significant trend toward improvement (mean difference 23.67 m, 95% CI −6.64 to 54.98, p=0.13) ( figure 4 ). Overall, treatment effects on this parameter appeared limited, as no significant differences were observed before and after therapy. For rituximab, mean walking distance remained stable (393±90 m at baseline vs 414±86 m at follow-up, p>0,05). Similarly, in both studies evaluating JAKi, 6MWT values showed no significant change over time, suggesting preservation rather than improvement of exercise capacity. HRCT Assessment of ILD progression by HRCT or microCT was reported in several studies, but with substantial heterogeneity in both methodology and results. Some studies relied on qualitative radiological evaluation, whereas others applied semi-quantitative or automated quantitative scoring systems. The timing of follow-up assessments also varied widely, from 6 months to more than 36 months. Across studies, treatment effects were inconsistent. In most cases, pulmonary findings remained stable under therapy, as evidenced—when available—by quantitative or semi-quantitative analyses. The proportions of patients classified as improved, stable or worsened varied considerably between cohorts and treatment classes. Stability was the most common outcome, although reported improvement rates ranged from approximately 6% to 30%, depending on the scoring method and therapeutic agent evaluated. Rituximab and abatacept cohorts provided the largest datasets, yet inter-study comparisons remain challenging because of methodological variability ( table 2 ). Overall, the marked heterogeneity in imaging endpoints and assessment techniques precludes firm conclusions regarding the impact of individual targeted therapies on HRCT-defined ILD progression. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the results, taking into account baseline lung involvement severity (FVC<80% predicted), studies with more than 20 patients, and assessments at 12 months. Sensitivity analysis for DAS28 was not feasible, as values remained above 3.2 in all included studies. 17 20 22 24 28 29 In patients classified as severe, with FVC assessed only at baseline, only studies evaluating rituximab were available. 21 23 24 28 31 No significant change in FVC was observed in this subgroup, whereas a significant improvement in DLCO was noted (mean difference +5.85, 95% CI 0.86 to 10.83, p=0.02) ( onlinesupplemental figures 3 4 ). Further sensitivity analyses restricted to studies with more than 20 patients and a 12 month follow-up did not reveal any significant differences, including for treatments with rituximab, abatacept or JAK inhibitors. No significant changes were observed for either FVC or DLCO ( onlinesupplemental figures 5 9 ). Discussion We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of bDMARDs and tsDMARDs on functional parameters in RA-ILD. The results of our meta-analysis indicate that these treatments are generally associated with the stabilisation of key pulmonary function parameters, namely FVC and DLCO. In addition, our systematic review of the literature revealed stability in other clinical or imaging outcomes, including HRCT findings and 6 min walk test performance. While rituximab appeared to be the most effective treatment across studies, this observation did not reach statistical significance. It is important to note that only rituximab was associated with a significant improvement in DLCO in patients with baseline FVC below 80%. In clinical practice, achieving stability in FVC and DLCO likely reflects a meaningful attenuation of fibrotic progression rather than complete reversibility, particularly in UIP-dominant RA-ILD. We also performed an analysis of the 6MWT, an important parameter reflecting the functional impact of RA-ILD. Although the number of available studies is small, these results indicate that current therapies may help maintain functional status in RA-ILD without translating into measurable gains in walking performance. Larger and longer-term studies will be required to clarify whether specific agents can improve exercise tolerance beyond stabilisation. RA-ILD is an increasingly recognised complication of rheumatoid arthritis, associated with excess mortality and substantial management challenges. 2 34 In daily clinical practice, treatment decisions in this population are often made without strong supporting evidence, as randomised controlled trials (RCTs) specifically targeting RA-ILD remain unavailable. Nonetheless, recent international guidelines have begun to acknowledge the importance of RA-ILD and offer preliminary therapeutic recommendations. 10 35 This highlights the need for evidence-based guidance in this complex population and underscores the relevance of synthesising available observational data to inform clinical decision-making. Our systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that all treatment classes show comparable effects on key pulmonary outcomes. Although rituximab demonstrated a trend toward greater efficacy, this observation did not reach statistical significance and should therefore be interpreted with caution. Addressing the questions raised by this meta-analysis will require the conduct of randomised controlled trials. However, it will be essential to reduce heterogeneity among included patients, particularly with regard to RA disease duration, duration of lung involvement and ILD pattern. In our meta-analysis, specific data on early RA-associated ILD were rarely available, as most included cohorts comprised patients with long-standing and heterogeneous disease durations. Pathophysiological mechanisms are unlikely to be identical across different stages of disease evolution, which may partly explain heterogeneity in treatment responses, as previously suggested in other RA outcomes. 36 Future RCTs should therefore include, at a minimum, patients with early-stage pulmonary involvement. This raises the important issue of screening for ILD in patients with RA, including those who are asymptomatic. To date, there are no recent consensus recommendations defining optimal screening strategies for RA-associated ILD. Nonetheless, recent prospective studies suggest that imaging-based approaches may allow the detection of subclinical ILD in RA, 37 39 supporting the rationale for earlier screening strategies in future trials. Screening approaches may reasonably be guided by established ILD risk factors, such as smoking status, male sex, late-onset RA and high ACPA titres. Our findings align with previous data, 11 while also offering several advances. Notably, this is the first meta-analysis to comprehensively include all bDMARD and tsDMARD classes, including TNFi and JAK inhibitors regardless of their selectivity. Although no therapeutic trial to date has directly compared JAK inhibitors to bDMARDs, our results suggest comparable efficacy across these treatment classes, in line with previous indirect comparisons. 12 It should be noted that not all studies evaluating JAK inhibitors could be included in the meta-analysis. Notably, the study by Kalyoncu et al , which could not be included in the meta-analysis, reported a marked improvement in FVC with tofacitinib. 40 However, our analysis did not assess the impact of conventional treatments, particularly methotrexate (or other csDMARDs) or glucocorticoids, on pulmonary function outcomes. Previous studies have suggested that methotrexate may influence the progression of RA-associated ILD. 41 However, recent data indicate that methotrexate does not appear to worsen RA-ILD. 42 Nevertheless, methotrexate is considered a cornerstone of RA management, and its use was broadly consistent across the included studies. Therefore, any potential confounding effect is likely to be limited. This study was conducted using a robust and transparent methodology. The systematic review adhered to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, 43 and three independent reviewers screened the literature in a blinded fashion to reduce selection bias. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus, and the risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-E tool, 44 enabling us to include studies with an overall low risk of bias. The meta-analysis was then conducted using the Cochrane Review Manager software (RevMan, V.5.3), ensuring standardised and reproducible statistical procedures. RA-ILD is a multifactorial condition influenced by age, smoking, high disease activity and the presence of ACPA and/or RF. 45 46 ACPA may promote local pulmonary inflammation through the recognition of citrullinated proteins in the lung. 47 48 Inducible bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (iBALT), enriched in T cells, B cells and follicular dendritic cells, has also been described in RA-ILD. 3 49 50 These ectopic lymphoid structures can act as germinal centres, 51 53 supporting local autoantibody production. This B cell-driven microenvironment may underlie the efficacy of B cell-depleting therapy such as rituximab. 54 However, several limitations of this work must be acknowledged. First, most of the included studies were observational and retrospective in design, with only a limited number of prospective cohorts. This introduces an inherent risk of selection bias and residual confounding despite the inclusion of studies with low overall bias. One potential source of bias is the lack of consideration of concomitant treatments that may influence the measured outcomes, particularly csDMARDs and glucocorticoids. To validate these findings and strengthen the evidence base, RCTs dedicated to RA-ILD are urgently needed. Second, the follow-up period was relatively short in most studies—typically between 6 and 12 months. Given the slow and heterogeneous progression of ILD, such timeframes may not adequately capture long-term pulmonary changes. Extended follow-up will be essential to assess the durability of treatment effects and better guide long-term management strategies. Third, an important limitation lies in the limited adjustment for potential confounding factors across studies. Variables such as smoking history, disease activity and autoantibody profiles were either inconsistently reported or not accounted for in analyses. These parameters are known to influence both ILD onset 55 58 and treatment response, 59 60 and their exclusion limits the interpretability and generalisability of the findings. Future research should aim to systematically integrate these variables into study design and analysis. Another important area for future investigation is the impact of treatment on RA-ILD subtypes. There are very limited data regarding treatment efficacy according to ILD pattern. In particular, evidence in patients with UIP is scarce, despite its recognised association with a poorer prognosis and reduced response to conventional therapies compared with NSIP. The most common radiological and histopathological patterns include usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), organising pneumonia (OP) and obliterative bronchiolitis. 61 However, few studies have evaluated differential treatment responses by ILD pattern. In one study of abatacept, no significant difference in efficacy was observed between UIP and NSIP subtypes. 17 It would be of interest to extend this analysis to other therapeutic agents to determine whether ILD pattern may influence treatment response and guide personalised therapy. In addition, the evolution of HRCT abnormalities under treatment remains insufficiently studied. We observed substantial heterogeneity and a lack of standardised imaging criteria in radiographic parameters assessed, which limits the interpretation of treatment effects on structural lung changes. The future application of artificial intelligence (AI)—particularly deep learning approaches applied to HRCT—offers promising perspectives in this area. AI-based tools could enable objective, reproducible and sensitive assessments of ILD extent and progression over time. 62 63 By improving standardisation and accuracy in radiographic evaluation, these technologies may contribute to the development of imaging-based endpoints and better therapeutic monitoring. In conclusion, targeted therapies—including both bDMARDs and tsDMARDs—appear to preserve pulmonary function in most patients with RA-ILD. While rituximab and JAKi show the most consistent signals of benefit, no statistically significant superiority emerged across treatment classes. Stabilisation of FVC and DLCO should therefore be considered a meaningful therapeutic goal in this population. Future research should focus on standardised, quantitative endpoints, longer follow-up and molecular stratification to guide personalised management of RA-ILD. documents.title: Prediction models for aspiration risk in stroke patients: a systematic review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death, with post-stroke dysphagia significantly increasing aspiration risk, leading to complications, such as aspiration pneumonia and higher mortality. Various prediction models for aspiration exist, but their clinical utility is limited by methodological heterogeneity.
AIM: This review aimed to evaluate the performance and applicability of these models for stroke patients, informing future model optimization and clinical use.
STUDY DESIGN: A comprehensive search was conducted across nine electronic databases until 20 January 2025. Studies on the development or validation of aspiration risk prediction models in adult stroke patients were included. Data extraction followed the CHARMS checklist, and bias risk and applicability were assessed using the PROBAST tool. The review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251007112).
RESULTS: Eighteen model development studies were included. Most demonstrated good discrimination (AUC/C-index: 0.756-0.955), with 16 showing good applicability. However, all studies had a high risk of bias, mainly due to retrospective designs, small sample sizes (events per variable < 20), inadequate missing data handling, univariate variable selection, and limited external validation. Key predictors included age, NIHSS score, Kubota Water Swallowing Test, history of aspiration, and Glasgow Coma Scale score.
CONCLUSION: Aspiration risk prediction models for stroke patients show promising predictive performance but are limited by methodological bias and heterogeneity. Future research should prioritize rigorous reporting and multi-center, large-sample external validation to improve model robustness and clinical applicability.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420251007112, URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420251007112.

The incidence of dysphagia has been reported to affect 42–67% of stroke patients within 3 days of onset, with nearly half of these patients being at a risk of aspiration ( 3 ). Aspiration is defined as the entry of food, liquid, saliva, or gastric contents into the airway (larynx, trachea, bronchi, or lungs) during feeding or non-fasting periods ( 4 ). Aspiration can precipitate severe complications, such as aspiration pneumonia and asphyxiation, significantly elevating patient mortality and healthcare expenditures ( 5 ). Therefore, early identification and the implementation of effective interventions for high-risk individuals are considered crucial strategies for mitigating aspiration risk in stroke patients. Aspiration risk prediction models serve as important tools for quantitatively estimating the probability of aspiration by integrating multidimensional predictors ( 6 ), such as demographic characteristics, current and past medical history, clinical assessments, and laboratory indicators. Currently, bedside swallowing screening, video fluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS), and fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) are commonly used to assess aspiration risk in patients with stroke ( 7 ). However, these approaches may be limited by operational complexity, resource requirements, and feasibility constraints for routine use in all stroke patients, while reliance solely on clinical experience may result in suboptimal accuracy. In recent years, various prediction models for aspiration risk in stroke patients have been developed worldwide. However, substantial heterogeneity exists in predictor selection, modeling methods, and target populations, and their methodological quality and clinical applicability have not been systematically synthesized and evaluated, which may limit their clinical implementation. A comprehensive evaluation of the predictive performance and application value of existing models may facilitate optimization of prediction tools and inform clinical decision-making. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically review aspiration risk prediction models in patients with stroke and to comprehensively analyze their predictive performance, methodological quality, and clinical utility, thereby providing evidence to support model optimization and early identification of high-risk populations in clinical practice. 2 Design and methods 2.1 Question formulation The research question for this systematic review was rigorously formulated based on the Population, Index prediction model, Comparator, Outcome, Timing, Setting (PICOTS) framework. The target population consisted of stroke patients, and the index intervention involved aspiration risk prediction models. No specific comparator was identified for this review. The primary outcome measure of interest was the incidence of aspiration in stroke patients, with models intended for application at the time of hospital admission. The relevant study settings included intensive care units, neurology wards, and neurosurgery wards. 2.2 Literature search A comprehensive systematic literature search was executed across several major electronic databases to identify pertinent studies: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, The Cochrane Library, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (ClNAHL), China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Database, China Science and Technology Journal Database (VIP), and SinoMed. The search encompassed studies published from each database’s inception up to January 2025. This systematic review has been prospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration number CRD420251007112. The search strategy was meticulously developed, employing a combination of controlled vocabulary [e.g., Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms] and free-text terms to ensure broad coverage of relevant literature. For searches conducted in Chinese databases, appropriate Chinese-language subject headings and keywords relevant to stroke, aspiration, and prediction models were utilized. Similarly, for English databases, comprehensive search terms were developed to capture studies on stroke, aspiration, and prediction models. These included MeSH terms and free-text keywords related to various forms of stroke (e.g., “stroke,” “cerebral hemorrhage,” and “brain infarction”), aspiration-related conditions (e.g., “aspiration” and “aspiration pneumonia”), and predictive modeling methodologies (e.g., “predictive value of tests,” “ROC curve,” “nomogram,” “machine learning,” and “prediction model”). The detailed strategies used for the search can be found in the Supplementary material . 2.3 Inclusion and exclusion criteria For the selection of relevant studies, specific inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied. Studies were included if they met the following conditions: (1) the study participants were stroke patients aged 18 years or older; (2) the research presented an original study focusing on the development or validation of aspiration risk prediction models for stroke patients; and (3) the study designs encompassed cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, or case–control studies. Conversely, studies were excluded if: (1) the prediction model incorporated fewer than two predictors; (2) the full text of the study could not be retrieved; or (3) the study was published in languages other than English or Chinese. 2.4 Literature screening and data extraction Literature screening and deduplication were systematically managed using EndNote bibliographic software. Initial screening of studies was performed based on titles and abstracts, followed by a thorough full-text review to confirm eligibility. A standardized data extraction form was specifically developed for this review, guided by the critical appraisal and data extraction for systematic reviews of prediction modelling studies (CHARMS) checklist ( 8 ). Data extraction and literature screening were independently conducted by two reviewers. Any discrepancies identified between the reviewers were meticulously resolved through consensus discussion or, when necessary, by arbitration from a third reviewer. 2.5 Risk of bias and applicability assessment of included literature The risk of bias and applicability of the included studies were rigorously assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) ( 9 ). The PROBAST framework assesses bias across four key domains: participants, predictors, outcome, and analysis, encompassing a total of 20 signaling questions. Similarly, applicability was evaluated across three corresponding domains: participants, predictors, and outcomes. These assessments were independently performed by two reviewers, and findings were meticulously recorded on standardized forms. Each signaling question was judged as ‘Yes,’ ‘Probably yes,’ ‘No,’ ‘Probably no,’ or ‘No information’ based on predefined criteria. The overall risk of bias for each domain was subsequently categorized as ‘Low,’ ‘High,’ or ‘Uncertain.’ Disagreements arising between the reviewers during this evaluation process were resolved through consensus discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. 3 Results 3.1 Study selection process and results An initial database search yielded 980 articles. Following a rigorous screening process based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 18 articles were ultimately included in this systematic review. Of these, 13 studies were published in Chinese, and 5 were published in English. The detailed study selection process, from initial retrieval to final inclusion, is visually depicted in Figure 1 . Figure 1 Flow chart of literature screening. Flowchart depicting the selection process for a systematic review: 980 records identified, 259 duplicates removed, 217 records screened, 692 excluded, 29 full texts reviewed, 11 more excluded, and 18 studies included in the final analysis. 3.2 Characteristics of included studies All 18 included studies were published within the last 3 years. Of these, 16 originated from China ( 10–25 ) and 2 from South Korea ( 26 , 27 ). Thirteen studies ( 10 , 12–15 , 17–24 ) were published in Chinese, while five ( 11 , 16 , 17 , 26 , 27 ) were published in English. Regarding study design, only one study ( 18 ) employed a cross-sectional design, and one ( 17 ) was a prospective cohort study; the remaining studies were retrospective in nature. In terms of outcome definitions, 12 studies ( 10 , 11 , 13 , 15 , 17–20 , 22 , 23 , 26 , 27 ) utilized a comprehensive definition of aspiration as the predicted outcome, whereas 6 studies ( 12 , 14 , 16 , 17 , 21 , 24 ) specifically predicted aspiration pneumonia as a distinct outcome. The sample sizes utilized for model construction ranged from 60 to 2,556 participants, with the number of events per variable (EPV) ranging from 1.318 to 24.889. Logistic regression modeling was employed in 16 studies ( 10–24 ). One study ( 26 ) integrated multiple machine learning methods, such as regularized logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, and Naive Bayes. Additionally, deep learning methods were utilized in one study ( 27 ). Regarding the handling of missing data, most studies did not report the presence or management of missing data; only one study ( 26 ) employed multiple imputation, while another ( 27 ) directly excluded cases with missing data. In terms of predictor variables, the number of candidate predictors considered ranged from 3 to 35. Continuous variables were appropriately handled in three studies ( 13 , 21 , 23 ). However, 16 of these studies ( 10 , 11 , 13–20 , 22–24 , 26 , 27 ) were deemed to have good applicability. The comprehensive results are summarized in Table 3 . 3.5.1 Bias risk assessment results In the participants’ domain, 16 studies ( 10–17 , 19–24 , 26 , 27 ) exhibited a high risk of bias. This was primarily due to their reliance on existing data for retrospective case analysis, which could lead to prediction results deviating from true clinical scenarios. In the predictors domain, 11 studies ( 10 , 12–14 , 17 , 20 , 21 , 23 , 24 , 26 , 27 ) were retrospective and did not clearly state whether predictors were assessed without knowledge of the outcome. Among these, five studies ( 10 , 14 , 21 , 23 , 24 ) did not provide detailed descriptions of the predictor measurement methods, leading to an “unclear” risk of bias assessment for this domain. In the outcome domain, one study ( 14 ) was rated as having a “high risk” of bias due to potential incorporation bias, where candidate predictors overlapped with the definition of the aspiration outcome. Additionally, five studies ( 10 , 13 , 20 , 21 , 24 ) did not clearly define the clinical outcome, resulting in an “unclear” rating, while the remaining studies in this domain were at low risk of bias. A high risk of bias was identified across all included studies in the analysis domain due to several common issues: (1) Except one study ( 26 ), the sample sizes in other studies were insufficient [events per variable (EPV) < 20], and no parameter adjustments were reported, potentially leading to underfitting or overfitting of the models. (2) In three studies ( 13 , 21 , 23 ), continuous variables were transformed into categorical variables, but no specific justification was provided for the threshold cut-off points used for categorization, which may have resulted in a loss of information. (3) Sixteen studies ( 10–24 ) did not report on missing data, and one study ( 27 ) employed complete case analysis, potentially introducing selection bias and overestimating model discriminatory ability. (4) Variable selection in 11 studies ( 10 , 13–15 , 17 , 19 , 20 , 22–24 , 27 ) was based solely on univariate analysis, failing to consider inter-variable interactions, which could lead to the omission of key predictors. (5) Six studies ( 13 , 17 , 21 , 23 , 26 , 27 ) did not provide an assessment of model calibration, and three studies ( 18 , 19 , 24 ) only reported the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, indicating incomplete calibration information. (6) Finally, 9 studies ( 10 , 12–14 , 19 , 21 , 23 , 27 ) did not perform internal validation, which could result in overly optimistic model performance estimates. 3.5.2 Applicability assessment results Of the 18 included studies, 2 ( 12 , 21 ) were assessed as having a high applicability risk due to their exclusive inclusion of patients older than 65 years. ( 16 ) High Low Low 4 Discussion 4.1 High risk of bias in aspiration risk prediction models for stroke patients Sixteen of the included studies ( 10–24 ) originated from China and were published within the last 3 years, indicating a growing focus on aspiration risk prediction models for stroke patients in China. However, all 18 included studies exhibited a high risk of bias, primarily attributable to methodological shortcomings that compromised their scientific rigor and robustness. The specific reasons are detailed as follows: First, most studies relied on retrospective data. While such data are readily accessible and cost-effective, their use is prone to selection and information biases, potentially leading to an overestimation of risk association strengths. Second, the majority of studies reported an events per variable (EPV) of less than 20. This inadequacy not only diminishes the model’s capacity to capture complex clinical relationships but also increases the likelihood of model overfitting or underfitting, thereby compromising its stability and accuracy ( 28 ). Third, conventional logistic regression methods were employed for model construction in 16 studies ( 10–24 ), with only 2 studies ( 26 , 27 ) exploring machine learning or deep learning approaches. While logistic regression is widely utilized in clinical practice, it presents inherent limitations in addressing non-linear relationships and variable interactions. Conversely, machine learning methods offer the potential to enhance predictive performance through feature engineering. Moreover, most studies failed to report on missing data, and only two studies ( 26 , 27 ) described their handling of missing data. Improper management of missing data can introduce selection bias and lead to information loss, consequently overestimating model discrimination. Future research is encouraged to utilize techniques such as multiple imputation or Bayesian models for missing data management, thereby ensuring data completeness and model reliability. Finally, external validation was conducted in only six studies ( 11 , 12 , 15 , 17–19 ), and these validations were limited to healthcare institutions of similar tiers or comparable populations. This limitation restricts the generalizability and transportability of the models across diverse geographical regions and patient populations ( 29 ). In summary, current models are still characterized by notable methodological limitations, particularly in study design rigor, sample size adequacy, missing data management, and external validation. Future studies should place greater emphasis on methodological standardization during model development and reporting to improve the scientific validity and reliability of prediction models. 4.2 Aspiration predictors in stroke patients exhibit good clinical effectiveness Early identification and intervention for high-risk factors in stroke patients are paramount for reducing the incidence of aspiration. This study identified age, NIHSS score, Kubota Water Swallowing Test, history of aspiration, and GCS score as the primary predictors of aspiration in stroke patients, consistent with findings from other studies ( 30 ). These factors not only possess biological plausibility but have also demonstrated clinical effectiveness, as validated by multiple studies. This suggests that clinical nurses should emphasize the assessment and prevention related to these characteristic variables. Age, identified as an independent risk factor for aspiration, is likely associated with diminished swallowing reflex, decreased coughing ability, and an increased burden of comorbidities in older patients. The NIHSS score, serving as an assessment tool for neurological deficits, is closely related to dysphagia. A study by Kumar et al. ( 31 ) involving 323 patients with acute ischemic stroke indicated that an NIHSS score of ≥12 was a significant predictor of persistent dysphagia, suggesting a higher aspiration risk for patients with elevated NIHSS scores. The Kubota Water Swallowing Test is widely recommended due to its simplicity and high sensitivity. However, its relatively low specificity may lead to an elevated false-positive rate; thus, modified versions of the Kubota Water Swallowing Test are frequently employed in clinical practice ( 32 ). Furthermore, international expert consensus recognizes a history of aspiration as a critical risk factor for aspiration in critically ill patients ( 33 ) because it reflects the previous impaired swallowing function. If this impaired state is not improved, it will continue to increase the risk of overt aspiration again ( 34 ). Additionally, a reduced GCS score is also considered a risk factor for aspiration, as it indicates impaired consciousness, which can suppress the cough reflex and pharyngeal sensory function, thereby increasing the risk of aspiration ( 35 ). Despite the demonstrated clinical effectiveness of these factors, their combined application necessitates careful consideration of clinical specificity and practicality. Currently, most studies primarily rely on clinical scales, with an evident lack of integrated analysis incorporating biomarkers and imaging features. Therefore, future research is advised to continue exploring the interactive effects of predictor variables and to construct multi-dimensional prediction systems, thereby optimizing model accuracy and utility to provide a scientific basis for individualized aspiration prevention strategies. 4.3 Sources of model heterogeneity and future optimization directions Current prediction models for aspiration risk in patients with stroke exhibit substantial heterogeneity in modeling approaches, outcome definitions, and study designs, which may contribute to variability in model performance and identified predictors. Most studies employed traditional logistic regression, whereas only a few applied machine learning techniques. Current evidence does not demonstrate a consistent advantage of advanced algorithms in predictive performance. Differences in feature selection procedures and model development strategies, together with limited sample sizes and insufficient external validation, further increase methodological heterogeneity and make direct comparisons across models difficult. Variability in outcome definitions also represents a major source of heterogeneity. In this review, the included studies predicted either aspiration or aspiration pneumonia. Aspiration reflects swallowing dysfunction and neurological impairment, whereas aspiration pneumonia is a secondary infectious complication influenced by additional factors such as inflammatory response and comorbidities. Consequently, models predicting aspiration more frequently incorporated neurological severity and swallowing-related variables, whereas those predicting aspiration pneumonia tended to include inflammatory markers and comorbidity-related factors. Inconsistent endpoint definitions, particularly the limited differentiation between symptomatic and asymptomatic aspiration, may therefore substantially influence predictor selection and model structure. Furthermore, most included studies adopted single-center retrospective designs, and high-quality prospective studies with rigorous external validation remain limited. The geographical distribution of the evidence was also highly concentrated, with most studies conducted in China and only a small number from other countries. Such concentration may limit the generalizability of existing models across different healthcare systems and patient populations. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome definitions, multicenter and multinational collaboration, and robust external validation, while optimizing modeling strategies under the premise of maintaining clinical interpretability, to enhance model robustness and cross-population applicability. 5 Conclusion This study systematically evaluated 18 included articles, revealing that existing aspiration risk prediction models for stroke patients generally demonstrate good predictive performance and applicability but are commonly associated with a high risk of bias. Furthermore, due to significant heterogeneity in model construction methods, predictor combinations, and outcome definitions, quantitative data synthesis was not conducted in this study. Consequently, the conclusions are based on qualitative analysis, which may limit the strength of the evidence. Future research should rigorously adhere to the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement to standardize study design and reporting. These findings may support early risk stratification of aspiration in stroke patients and provide a reference for future model development and clinical implementation. documents.title: Addressing the U.S. maternal health crisis: a systematic review of healthcare access barriers, disparate outcomes, and effective interventions.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The United States faces a profound maternal health crisis despite its global economic standing, with maternal mortality rates significantly higher than other high-income countries and stark disparities across racial and ethnic lines. This systematic literature review aims to synthesize current evidence on barriers to maternal healthcare access, resulting health outcomes, and effective interventions for reducing disparities.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, and ProQuest for literature published January 2000 and December 2024. The initial search yielded 122,756 records, which were narrowed to 44 studies for final synthesis after applying inclusion/exclusion criteria. Thematic analysis identified patterns related to barriers, outcomes, and interventions in maternal healthcare.
RESULTS: The systematic search identified 44 studies for synthesis. Analysis revealed five major barrier categories affecting maternal healthcare access: financial (24 references), systematic (34 references), educational (6 references), geographical (17 references), and comorbidity-related (1 reference). These barriers contributed to concerning disparities in maternal health outcomes, with Black women experiencing mortality rates 3-4 times higher than White women. Promising interventions included safety net providers (such as community health centers, mental health teams), culturally sensitive approaches, healthcare workers (doulas, translators), predictive models, special initiatives, and policy changes (Medicaid expansion, telehealth).
CONCLUSION: Addressing the U.S. maternal health crisis requires coordinated action targeting multifaceted barriers and implementing evidence-based interventions. Recommendations include expanding Medicaid coverage beyond the current postpartum limit, implementing approaches addressing social determinants of health, integrating diverse healthcare workers into maternal care teams, and prioritizing culturally sensitive, patient-informed care while actively addressing systematic barriers, particularly racism and discrimination.
documents.conclusions: Addressing the U.S. maternal health crisis requires coordinated action targeting multifaceted barriers and implementing evidence-based interventions. Recommendations include expanding Medicaid coverage beyond the current postpartum limit, implementing approaches addressing social determinants of health, integrating diverse healthcare workers into maternal care teams, and prioritizing culturally sensitive, patient-informed care while actively addressing systematic barriers, particularly racism and discrimination.

Background The United States faces a profound maternal health crisis despite its global economic standing, with maternal mortality rates significantly higher than other high-income countries and stark disparities across racial and ethnic lines. This systematic literature review aims to synthesize current evidence on barriers to maternal healthcare access, resulting health outcomes, and effective interventions for reducing disparities. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, and ProQuest for literature published January 2000 and December 2024. The initial search yielded 122,756 records, which were narrowed to 44 studies for final synthesis after applying inclusion/exclusion criteria. Thematic analysis identified patterns related to barriers, outcomes, and interventions in maternal healthcare. Results The systematic search identified 44 studies for synthesis. Analysis revealed five major barrier categories affecting maternal healthcare access: financial (24 references), systematic (34 references), educational (6 references), geographical (17 references), and comorbidity-related (1 reference). These barriers contributed to concerning disparities in maternal health outcomes, with Black women experiencing mortality rates 3-4 times higher than White women. Promising interventions included safety net providers (such as community health centers, mental health teams), culturally sensitive approaches, healthcare workers (doulas, translators), predictive models, special initiatives, and policy changes (Medicaid expansion, telehealth). Conclusion Addressing the U.S. maternal health crisis requires coordinated action targeting multifaceted barriers and implementing evidence-based interventions.
