conventional methods Three studies by Beighton et al. [ 33 ], Percival et al. [ 44 ], and Fure et al. [ 38 ] using saliva samples, both unstimulated and stimulated, reported significantly higher levels of Streptococcus mutans and lactobacilli in older adults compared to younger adults, suggesting an increased caries risk in older populations. The impact of denture use on the oral microbiome yielded conflicting results. While Beighton et al. and Percival et al. found no significant differences in Streptococcus mutans and lactobacilli levels between denture-wearing older adults and younger adults, Marsh et al. [ 41 ] and Fure et al. reported significant increases in these bacterial counts among denture users. In studies investigating periodontal pathogens, Savitt et al. [ 45 ] observed that older adults had significantly higher levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis , but significantly lower levels of Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans , compared to younger adults. In contrast, Haffajee et al. [ 39 ] found no significant differences in periodontal pathogens between older adults with well-maintained periodontium and periodontally healthy younger adults. Two studies by Fernandes et al. [ 36 ] and Kishi et al. [ 40 ] demonstrated significantly higher levels of periodontal pathogens in dentate older adults compared to edentulous individuals, indicating the continued relevance of periodontal microbial load in individuals with natural teeth. Senpuku et al. [ 46 ] reported that frail older adults were found to harbor higher levels of pneumonia-associated bacteria, including Staphylococcus spp ., Pseudomonas spp., and Candida albicans . Similarly, Chen et al. [ 35 ] found that individuals with oral frailty exhibited a greater proportion of pneumonia-associated bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Serratia marcescens . Notably, both studies also reported increased levels of Enterobacterales in individuals with frailty and oral frailty. Studies by Tada et al. [ 47 ] and Ortega et al. [ 43 ] reported that older adults with swallowing difficulties had significantly elevated levels of opportunistic pathogens, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , emphasizing the increased risk of pneumonia in individuals with frailty, oral frailty, or swallowing dysfunction. Findings from 16S rRNA sequencing methods Alpha-diversity Alpha-diversity encompasses different indices (e.g., Observed OTU, Chao1, Shannon, and Simpson) that weight richness and evenness differently and can respond differently to preprocessing and taxonomic resolution. Therefore, the direction and size of age- or frailty-associated effects may depend on the chosen metric, and measures may not show a positive linear relationship. Findings on alpha-diversity were inconsistent across studies comparing older adults with younger or middle-aged adults, with variability also influenced by sample type and taxonomic resolution used in the analysis. Detailed alpha-diversity findings and the indices used for measurement are summarized (see Additional file 3). Four studies reported decreased alpha-diversity (reflecting both richness and evenness) in older adults compared to young adults [ 54 , 55 , 59 , 66 ], three found no significant differences [ 56 , 62 , 64 ], and one observed an increase in diversity [ 58 ]. When comparing older adults with middle-aged adults, one study reported a reduction in diversity [ 59 ], while another found no significant difference [ 53 ]. In a study by Guo et al. [ 51 ], which included three age groups of older adults aged 65–80 years, no significant change in diversity was observed. Interestingly, studies by Wu et al. [ 62 ] and Ji et al. [ 52 ] found that long-lived older adults exhibited reduced alpha-diversity compared to normal older adults. Regarding frailty, Ogawa et al. [ 58 ] reported a significant reduction in diversity at the phylum level among frail older adults. However, no significant differences were observed at deeper taxonomic levels (genus and species) in studies by both Ogawa et al. and Larson et al. [ 54 ]. In contrast, edentulism, having fewer than 20 teeth, and the presence of dry mouth were consistently associated with reduced alpha-diversity across multiple studies [ 50 , 64 ]. Beta-diversity Beta-diversity is similarly method-dependent, with results varying according to the distance metric used (e.g., Bray–Curtis versus weighted or unweighted UniFrac), whether analyses emphasize abundance or presence/absence data, and how compositionality and normalization are handled. As a result, studies may detect (or miss) group separation depending on the chosen dissimilarity measure and ordination or statistical testing approach. Detailed beta-diversity findings and the metrics used for measurement are summarized in (see Additional file 4). Beta-diversity results were also mixed when comparing older and younger adults. Five studies reported significant differences in community composition [ 54 – 56 , 59 , 61 ], while two studies found no significant differences [ 62 , 63 ]. Similarly, when comparing older adults to middle-aged adults, one study reported a significant difference [ 53 ], and another reported none [ 59 ]. Interestingly, Schwartz et al. [ 59 ] found significant differences between older and young adults but no difference between older and middle-aged adults. When comparing among three age groups of older adults aged 65–80 years [ 51 ], as well as older adults versus long-lived older adults, there were no significant differences in beta-diversity [ 52 , 62 ]. More consistent differences were observed between frail and non-frail older adults. Studies by Ogawa et al. [ 58 ], Yang et al. [ 65 ], and Larson et al. [ 54 ] reported significant shifts in microbial community composition associated with frailty. Additionally, Gazdeck et al. [ 50 ] reported significant differences between edentulous and dentate older adults. Relative abundance of taxa Distinct trends of relative abundance of taxa varied between two main comparison groups: (i) older adults versus younger adults, and (ii) older adults versus frailty, edentulism, or fewer than 20 teeth. At the phylum level, Bacillota was found to be less abundant in older adults [ 55 , 63 ] but more abundant in frail [ 57 ] and edentulous individuals [ 50 ]. Similarly, Streptococcus (within Bacillota) followed this trend, with an additional study reporting higher abundance in long-lived older adults [ 52 ] and individuals with fewer than 20 teeth [ 64 ]. Veillonella (also within Bacillota) showed reduced abundance in older adults [ 55 , 58 ] but increased abundance in frail individuals [ 57 ]. Likewise, Haemophilus (within Pseudomonadota) was found to be less abundant in older adults [ 56 , 62 ] but more abundant in frailty [ 57 ]. In contrast, Bacteroidota was more abundant in older adults [ 55 , 63 ] but less abundant in frail individuals [ 57 ]. Prevotella (within Bacteroidota) reflected this trend and was also found to be less abundant in edentulous older adults [ 50 ]. Interestingly, Prevotella and Tannerella (both within Bacteroidota) were more abundant in older adults but less abundant in long-lived individuals [ 52 ]. Some genera demonstrated opposing abundance trends in frail versus edentulous individuals. For example, Veillonella (within Bacillota) and Actinomyces (within Actinomycetota) were more abundant in frail older adults [ 57 ] but less abundant in edentulous older adults [ 50 ]. In addition, when comparing among three age groups of older adults aged 65–80 years, there were no significant differences in abundance taxa [ 51 ]. A few taxa showed similar trends across both comparison groups. Selenomonas (within Bacillota) was more abundant in both older adults [ 58 , 66 ] and frail individuals [ 57 ]. In contrast, Fusobacterium (within Fusobacteriota) and Campylobacter (within Campylobacteriota) were less abundant in older adults [ 55 , 58 , 66 ] and in frail individuals [ 57 ]. Additionally, Capnocytophaga (within Bacteroidota) and Fusobacterium showed consistently lower abundance in frail individuals [ 57 ] and those with fewer than 20 teeth [ 64 ]. Other relative abundance taxa findings with inconsistent patterns across studies are presented (see Additional file 5). Due to the limitation of species-level detection by metagenomic analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing and inconsistent findings between the studies, species-level results were omitted from the summary [ 67 ]. Age-associated patterns in alpha-diversity and taxa Several studies that included participants spanning from childhood to older adulthood investigated associations between microbial taxa and age. Four studies using different sample types found a positive association between alpha-diversity and increasing age [ 49 , 60 , 61 , 63 ], with the exception of one study by Yang et al. [ 65 ], which did not support this trend. Notably, Yang et al. also found a positive association between number of teeth and alpha-diversity (Shannon and Simpson). In contrast, three studies reported a negative association between frailty and alpha diversity [ 49 , 60 , 65 ]. At the genus level, four taxa were consistently associated with aging across multiple studies: Veillonella [ 49 , 60 ], Granulicatella [ 61 , 63 ], Prevotella [ 51 , 52 , 61 ], Alloprevotella [ 49 , 61 ], and Haemophilus [ 60 , 61 ] showed negative associations with increasing age. While Comamonas [ 60 , 61 ] showed a positive association with age. Other genera with inconsistent findings across studies are summarized (see Additional file 6). Risk of bias The risk of bias among studies utilizing conventional microbiological methods was assessed as primarily low in 11 studies, while five studies were rated as having a moderate risk of bias [ 37 , 40 , 42 , 45 , 46 ]. Similarly, among studies employing 16S rRNA gene sequencing methods, 14 studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias, and four studies were rated as moderate [ 49 , 58 , 60 , 65 ]. Although studies comparing older adults with younger or middle-aged adults regarding alpha- and beta-diversity remain inconclusive, differences in taxonomic abundance were observed, indicating that microbial changes occur with aging. During healthy aging, marked differences in microbial diversity or taxonomic abundance may not be evident until very advanced age (e.g., > 85 years), at which point a reduction in alpha-diversity may occur while beta-diversity remains relatively stable. In contrast, frail older adults exhibit significant changes in beta-diversity from healthy aging, despite non-significant changes in alpha-diversity. This pattern suggests that frailty may be associated with a restructuring of community composition (i.e., which taxa dominate and how individuals differ from one another) rather than a uniform change in within-sample richness or evenness. Taken together, the oral microbiome of older adults may shift toward an adapted community consistent with the natural resilience of the oral microbiome [ 1 ]. In contrast, the microbiome of frail individuals tends to shift toward a microbial imbalance, demonstrated by a reduction in taxa important for biofilm formation and an increase in pathogenic taxa. This phenomenon may also be explained by the reduced ability to maintain oral hygiene, which facilitates the overgrowth of pathogenic taxa, while a reduced number of teeth results in the loss of oral niches. Furthermore, oral hypofunction, which commonly co-occurs with frailty, can further restrict eating ability, diminish natural self-cleaning mechanisms, and weaken protective oral defenses, collectively accelerating microbial imbalance. Taxonomic abundance potentially associated with oral microbial dysbiosis At the phylum level, similar to the gut microbiome, Bacillota decreases, while Bacteroidota increases with aging [ 68 ]. Interestingly, a reverse trend is observed in frail individuals, supporting the concept of dysbiosis. Additionally, frail individuals show reduced levels of Fusobacterium and Campylobacter , both of which play essential roles in biofilm formation, suggesting potential disruption of biofilm stability. In particular, Fusobacterium nucleatum is considered a key bridging organism in dental plaque maturation, and its depletion may therefore influence overall community organization [ 69 , 70 ]. Studies found that Streptococcus and Veillonella , which typically decrease with age, show an increase in frail older adults. This shift could reflect poor oral hygiene and the development of a dysbiotic biofilm in this population. Streptococcus is a core early colonizer in the oral cavity, and Veillonella utilizes lactate produced by Streptococcus , suggesting a metabolic cross-feeding process in dysbiosis [ 71 ]. Interestingly, Singh et al. [ 72 ] found that Streptococcus was significantly increased in the oral microbiome of unhealthy compared to healthy aging cohorts. However, Streptococcus could also increase in older adults with edentulism or fewer than 20 teeth, regardless of frailty [ 50 , 64 , 73 ]. Moreover, frail older adults, especially those with fewer teeth, showed microbial shifts similar to those seen in individuals with edentulism. This highlights the potential overlap between frailty and edentulism, where the loss of oral niches and functional decline both contribute to microbial dysbiosis. Interestingly, Veillonella (within Bacillota) was higher when Fusobacterium (within Fusobacteriota) was lower in frail compared to non-frail individuals, indicating specific microbial signatures of frailty. Findings from Kageyama et al. [ 74 ] explained that older adults have two community types: type I, who are dominated with Veillonella and Prevotella, exhibit a higher risk of all-cause death and pneumonia-related death than type II, who are dominated with Fusobacterium and Neisseria . Prevotella increases with aging but decreases in frail individuals, a pattern also observed in the gut microbiome [ 13 ]. The study exploring older adults with more than 26 teeth and no periodontal disease reported that their relative abundance and metabolome profiles resembled those of young adults with periodontal disease, yet remained distinct from periodontal-healthy young adults [ 56 ]. Supporting this, Kametani et al. [ 75 ] demonstrated that red complex species ( P. gingivalis, T. forsythia , and T. denticola ) play an important role in uniquely shaping the oral microbiome in a frail cohort, although periodontal disease developed only in those who harbor all of these species. In addition, a study found that a higher proportion of Prevotella in older adults was associated with oral frailty, particularly in those with subjective swallowing problems, compared to those with lower or middle levels [ 76 ]. Conversely, reduced Prevotella abundance has been linked to an increased risk of pneumonia [ 77 ]. Enterobacterales, opportunistic pathogens associated with pneumonia, has been reported in frail and oral frail older adults. These bacteria, often introduced from the respiratory tract, are known to pose a risk of aspiration pneumonia, particularly in individuals with dysphagia [ 78 ]. However, sequencing studies have not consistently shown the same overgrowth of Enterobacterales in frail adults. Instead, Haemophilus (within Pseudomonadota), a generally commensal organism in the oral cavity, showed higher abundance in these individuals, potentially reflecting oro-respiratory overlap and contributing to the development of aspiration pneumonia. Notably, Jiang et al. [ 79 ] found that caries-free older adults exhibited a more complex bacterial community, with an enriched proportion of Pseudomonadota and Haemophilus , compared to caries-active older adults. At the cellular level, this potential dysbiosis, together with an increased abundance of oral pathogens, may contribute to the production of metabolites and virulence factors that aggravate senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) activity in senescent cells, thereby promoting systemic chronic inflammation (inflammaging) [ 80 ]. This proposed interaction is in line with the oral microbiome–SASP–aging axis and may be relevant to frailty as well as other age-related conditions [ 81 ]. Oral factors potentially contributing to oral microbiome changes The inconsistency in alpha diversity results when comparing older adults to younger adults may be attributed to several confounding factors, particularly the number of remaining teeth. Studies that report reduced diversity in older adults often include participants with fewer teeth, resulting in fewer niches for oral bacteria, further promoting dysbiosis [ 82 , 83 ]. For example, Yamamoto et al. [ 64 ] observed no significant differences in diversity between younger adults and older adults with more than 20 teeth, whereas those with fewer than 20 teeth had reduced diversity. Similarly, Nishimoto et al. [ 56 ] found no significant differences in diversity between older adults with more than 26 teeth and younger adults. Furthermore, Yang et al. [ 65 ] proposed a potential mechanistic pathway in which a reduced number of teeth is associated with decreased oral microbiome diversity, ultimately contributing to frailty. The oral microbiome diversity in older adults with dry mouth was lower than those without dry mouth. These environmental changes impact the habitat of the oral microbiome and are reflected in the study using tongue plaque samples. Saliva plays an important role in the oral microbiome, such as providing nutrients, clearing microorganisms, and containing antimicrobial factors that manipulate the composition of microbes [ 84 ]. Many studies also support the difference between individuals with and without hyposalivation, as demonstrated in patients with xerostomia [ 85 ], hyposalivation and salivary pH [ 73 ], and Sjögren syndrome [ 86 ]. This finding supports the unstable outcomes from using saliva samples from the older adults, especially when salivary problems were not addressed in the previous studies. Findings from studies using conventional methods show conflicting evidence regarding the impact of dentures on the oral microbiome, whereas a metagenomic study found a higher prevalence of pathogenic bacteria in individuals wearing removable partial dentures compared with dentate older adults without dentures [ 87 ]. Additionally, the number of natural teeth retained by denture wearers and the material of complete dentures have been shown to influence the oral microbiome [ 82 , 88 ]. Overall, the effect of dentures on the oral microbiome remains inconclusive and needs further investigation. Denture wearing often co-occurs with poor oral health and candidiasis, which is associated with a dysbiotic bacterial community. Candida spp. are of particular concern given the increasing spread of antifungal resistance, including C. auris, in nursing home settings [ 89 ]. Asakawa et al. [ 83 , 90 ] reported an overgrowth of non-albicans Candida species in older adults, while Kraneveld et al. [ 91 ] found that microbiomes with a high Candida load were less diverse and showed distinct enrichment of Streptococcus . These findings parallel what is observed in frail, edentulous, and reduced-tooth populations in the current review. Although evidence remains mixed, the recurring association between dentures, pathogenic or opportunistic taxa, and reduced diversity underscores the importance of further research into how denture use, hygiene practices, and material type shape the oral microbiome. Notably, the study by Sekundo et al. [ 73 ] in a centenarian cohort found that factors such as degree of disability, nursing care, diabetes, and smoking did not significantly impact the oral microbiome. However, maintaining good oral health, particularly through regular dental visits, had a positive influence on microbial diversity. These findings highlight the need for researchers to carefully select exclusion criteria when studying the oral microbiome in older adults. Compared with younger populations, older adults present more complex and variable oral and systemic conditions that can easily confound microbiome outcomes, making rigorous study design essential for answering research questions accurately. Limitations A key limitation of oral microbiome research is the substantial methodological heterogeneity across studies, including variability in pre-analytical and analytical procedures, which reduces reproducibility [ 92 ]. Currently, there is no gold standard or consensus protocol for oral microbiome study, which contributes to variability in study design, sequencing approaches, bioinformatic pipelines, reported outcomes, and the handling of confounding factors. Consequently, the comparison of findings from sequencing studies must be interpreted with caution [ 29 – 31 ]. Frailty is a time-dependent condition, and the lack of longitudinal evidence limits the ability to determine whether oral microbiome dysbiosis contributes to the development of frailty or whether frailty itself drives microbial changes. Therefore, well-designed longitudinal studies are essential to clarify the causal pathways between oral microbiome alterations and frailty progression. In addition, further investigation of other aspects of oral hypofunction should be examined to better identify oral factors associated with changes in the oral microbiome. Implications for research Due to inconsistent findings between studies using saliva samples, tongue samples may be more reliable for oral microbiome studies, as different tongue coatings share a similar overall microbial composition but differ in relative abundance, which can reflect the risk of certain diseases [ 93 ]. Moreover, the tongue microbiome closely mirrors the saliva microbiome in healthy individuals [ 94 – 96 ]. Therefore, using tongue samples may be a better choice for studying the oral microbiome of older adults, who frequently experience hyposalivation, helping to avoid this important confounding factor. In addition, studies targeted different 16S rRNA variable regions, which substantially influence taxonomic resolution and detection accuracy. Evidence comparing the performance of these regions suggests that V1–V2 provides the more reliable coverage for the oral and nasal microbiome [ 97 , 98 ], while full-length 16S sequencing can offer even broader resolution by capturing all variable regions [ 99 ]. Variation in the reference database further influences taxonomic findings. Suggested optimal taxonomic assignment depends on matching the sequencing region to an appropriate database, for example, Greengenes2 for V3–V4 or V4 regions, and HOMD for V1–V2 [ 100 ]. Overall, greater standardization of pre-analytical procedures, sequencing strategies, and bioinformatic pipelines is needed to improve reproducibility and comparability in oral microbiome research. An additional methodological consideration is the availability of raw sequencing data from the included studies. Publicly accessible datasets would facilitate secondary analyses using uniform bioinformatic pipelines and standardized reference databases, which could reduce methodological heterogeneity and improve comparability across studies [ 101 ]. This approach may also enable pooled analyses and the application of quantitative dysbiosis indices, such as the Subgingival Microbial Dysbiosis Index (SMDI) and its extensions to saliva and tongue microbiomes, to better explore the relationship between periodontitis-associated microbiome dysbiosis and unhealthy aging [ 102 , 103 ]. Future studies should therefore prioritize data sharing. Although current evidence suggests possible associations between certain oral microbiome profiles and frailty or oral frailty, these observations remain preliminary. Given the heterogeneity of the available studies and the lack of longitudinal data, no clear microbial signature specific to or predictive of unhealthy aging can currently be identified. Higher-resolution microbiome analyses, ideally at the species or strain level, together with standardized study designs, may help clarify these associations. Furthermore, longitudinal studies are required to determine whether these microbial changes are simply correlated with frailty or play a causal role. Such evidence will be necessary before considering the development of microbial biomarkers or microbiome-targeted interventions. Conclusions Frailty and having fewer teeth appear to exert a stronger influence on the oral microbiome than healthy aging. While older adults may develop a microbial community distinct from that of younger adults, frailty is associated with a microbial imbalance, demonstrated by a reduction in taxa important for biofilm formation and an increase in pathogenic taxa. Similar patterns are observed in individuals with fewer teeth, though evidence linking other aspects of oral hypofunction remains limited. Supplementary Information Additional file 1. documents.title: Efficacy and Safety of Hospital-at-Home versus Traditional Hospital Care in Older Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
documents.abstract:
Introduction: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the Hospital-at-Home (HaH) model compared to traditional hospital care for older patients.
METHODS: We comprehensively searched PubMed, Embase, Medline, Cochrane Library, SinoMed, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to April 15, 2024. The primary outcomes were length of stay (LOS) and readmission rates. Secondary outcomes included total cost, mortality, adverse events, and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL).
RESULTS: Eleven RCTs involving 3,301 patients were included. The HaH group demonstrated a significantly shorter LOS (SMD = -0.45; 95% CI: -0.62 to -0.28; p < 0.01) and lower total healthcare costs (SMD = -0.40; 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.28; p < 0.0001) than the traditional care group. HaH was also associated with a reduced risk of readmission, with subgroup analyses showing consistent benefits at 1, 3, and 9 months. Additionally, patients receiving HaH showed modest but significant improvements in IADL scores (SMD = -0.15; 95% CI: -0.26 to -0.04; p < 0.0001). However, no significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of mortality (RR = 1.03; 95% CI: 0.49-2.18; p = 0.93) or adverse event rates (RR = 1.01; 95% CI: 0.43-2.36; p = 0.084).
CONCLUSION: For a selected group of older patients, HaH appears to be a viable alternative to traditional hospitalization, offering advantages in reducing LOS, healthcare costs, and readmission rates, while potentially improving functional recovery without increasing risks to patient safety. Further research is warranted to confirm these findings and refine implementation strategies. .

Keywords Hospital-at-Home Inpatient Aged Randomize controlled trials This study was not supported by any sponsor or funder. pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf no pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC accessibilitySummary WCAG 2.1 Level AA accessibility-pdf-ua-compliance yes Introduction The aging global population is driving a substantial increase in healthcare utilization, characterized by high rates of emergency department visits and hospital readmissions among older adults, which places unsustainable strain on healthcare systems [ 1 – 3 ]. Exacerbated by bed shortages and workforce limitations, this strain compromises care quality and patient outcomes [ 4 , 5 ]. In response, innovative care models like Hospital-at-Home (HaH) have emerged as a critical alternative. HaH is a structured service model designed to deliver acute, hospital-level care as a substitutive alternative to traditional inpatient admission. It involves the active provision of comprehensive treatment by healthcare professionals (e.g., physicians, nurses, therapists) in the patient’s own home, typically including components such as remote monitoring, intravenous therapies, and scheduled visits. This model operates primarily through two pathways: admission avoidance (initiating care directly at home for eligible patients) and early discharge (facilitating continued hospital-level care at home following initial stabilization in the hospital) [ 6 , 7 ]. This model aligns with the preferences of many older patients to receive care at home and may reduce the risk of hospital-acquired complications [ 8 , 9 ]. While existing evidence suggests HaH can reduce costs and maintain care quality for selected acutely ill adults [ 10 , 11 ], its safety and efficacy for the more vulnerable older population – who are at higher risk of iatrogenic harm and functional decline – remain a subject of concern and incomplete understanding [ 12 ]. A comprehensive evaluation comparing HaH to traditional inpatient care for this demographic is therefore necessary. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HaH for older patients. We specifically examined critical outcomes including length of stay (LOS), readmission rates, total costs, mortality, and functional status (instrumental activities of daily living, IADL). This synthesis aims to provide a robust evidence base to guide clinicians and policymakers and to identify key areas for future research and model optimization. Methods This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251238936). Eligibility Criteria Population Older patients who were eligible for hospital care at home did not require ongoing acute hospital-based treatment (as judged by a consultant geriatrician) and consented to being treated at home. Older adults in this review were defined as individuals aged ≥65 years or studies where the proportion of older participants was more than 80%. This dual criterion was applied to include studies that primarily focused on an older population, even if the mean age was not explicitly above 65 years. We excluded adults under 50 years old and those residing in rehabilitation centers, nursing homes, or other healthcare facilities. Intervention The intervention group comprised patients eligible for HaH interventions, regardless of where they were assessed or treated. HaH interventions could admit patients directly from the community, avoiding hospital contact, or from the emergency room or an acute assessment unit. HaH was defined as a service model that provides active, hospital-level treatment by healthcare professionals in the patient’s home for conditions that would otherwise require acute inpatient care. This encompasses both admission avoidance models (where care is initiated directly at home) and early discharge models (where patients are stabilized in the hospital before transitioning home). The interventions typically involved a multidisciplinary team (e.g., physicians, nurses, physical therapists) and could include components such as remote vital signs monitoring, intravenous medication administration, and scheduled home visits. Comparator Only studies with control groups receiving care exclusively in hospital wards were included. Outcomes Primary outcomes included LOS and total cost. Secondary outcomes included mortality, readmission rates, adverse events, and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). Study Selection We included RCTs based on the implementation of the HaH model in older patients. HaH was defined as detailed above. Interventions delivered in outpatient settings, nursing institutions for the aged, or primarily involving patient self-care at home were excluded. Studies involving patients admitted due to worsening severe illness were also excluded. Search Strategy We conducted a comprehensive search of several major databases to identify relevant publications for our review. This included searching Web of Science (which encompasses the Web of Science Core Collection, MEDLINE, Embase, and the SciELO Citation Index), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Our search was conducted from the inception of these databases up until April 30, 2024. To ensure we captured all ongoing studies, we also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. In addition to these database searches, we reviewed the reference lists of relevant Cochrane Reviews to identify any additional studies that might have been missed in our initial searches. The search strategy for PubMed is provided as an example: (“Hospital-at-Home” [Mesh] OR “HaH” OR “home hospitalization”) AND (“Aged” [Mesh] OR “elderly” OR “older adult”) AND (“Randomized Controlled Trial” [ptyp]). Similar strategies adapted to the syntax of each database were used and are available in the online supplementary Material S1 (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000551394 ). Data Extraction To systematically collect and organize data from the included studies, we utilized a structured data extraction form. This form was designed to capture the following details. Participant Characteristics We recorded the title of the study, the name of the first author, the design of the study (such as RCT), and the publication time (year of publication). Basic Information of Study Subjects We documented the sample size of the study, the age range or mean age of the participants, the sex distribution, the type of disease or condition being studied, and the form of intervention being tested (such as medication, surgery, or behavioral therapy). Outcomes and Measures We extracted data on several key outcomes, including LOS, rates of readmission, total cost of care, mortality rates, and the level of independence as measured by instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). Data extraction was performed by two independent reviewers to ensure accuracy and minimize bias. In cases where there were disagreements between the two reviewers, these were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer to reach a consensus. Quality Appraisal Two independent researchers conducted a thorough evaluation of the quality of the studies that were included in the analysis. They utilized the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [ 13 ], which is a well-established and widely recognized method for assessing the quality of research studies. This tool was specifically designed to evaluate various aspects of study design and conduct that could potentially introduce bias into the results. The researchers looked at several key components, including the methods used for random distribution of subjects, the concealment of allocation to ensure that the groups being compared were treated equally, the effectiveness of blinding procedures to prevent knowledge of group assignments from influencing the outcomes, the integrity of the data collected, and selective reporting, which refers to the practice of only reporting outcomes that are favorable to the hypothesis being tested. In addition to these, other sources of bias were also considered. Each study was then rated on a scale that indicated whether it had a low, high, or unclear risk of bias in these areas. To ensure the accuracy and consistency of the evaluations, any disagreements that arose between the two researchers were resolved through a collaborative discussion with a third independent reviewer. Data Synthesis and Reporting This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. The PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as online supplementary Material S3. To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of hospital care at home versus traditional hospital care in older patients, we conducted comprehensive meta-analyses using Stata 18 statistical software (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Continuous outcome measures were analyzed using mean differences with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), while dichotomous outcomes were assessed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. The presence and degree of heterogeneity across studies were systematically evaluated through the chi-square test (with statistical significance set at p < 0.10) and quantified using the I 2 statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across studies attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance. Based on these assessments, we employed a fixed-effect model (Mantel-Haenszel method) when minimal heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 ≤ 50%), while a random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method) was utilized in cases of substantial heterogeneity ( I 2 > 50%) [ 14 ]. All statistical tests were two tailed, with the threshold for statistical significance established at α = 0.05. The results of these analyses were visually represented through forest plots, which provide a graphical display of effect estimates from individual studies along with their CI and the pooled estimate. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of our findings by sequentially excluding each study and examining the impact on overall effect sizes. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test when more than 10 studies were available for a given outcome. Results Literature Search and Screening Results During the initial phase of our research, a comprehensive search was conducted, which yielded a total of 3,227 articles from various databases and resources. Following a rigorous screening process, which involved the application of specific inclusion and exclusion criteria, 11 RCTs were ultimately selected for inclusion in our systematic review [ 9 – 12 , 15 – 21 ]. This selection process is visually represented in Figure 1 . Fig. 1. Study selection flowchart. Flowchart shows study selection process for a systematic review. Records were identified from four databases (PubMed, n=323; Web of Science, n=2,588; Cochrane Library, n=311; Sinomed, n=5), totaling 3,227. After removing 220 duplicate records before screening, titles and abstracts of 3,007 remaining records were screened, and 2,711 were excluded as irrelevant. Full - texts of 296 articles were assessed for eligibility. 285 were excluded due to reasons like not being a randomized controlled trial (n=78), unrelated intervention (n=100), etc. Finally, 11 studies were included in the review. Study Characteristics These studies, which were conducted with a total of 3,301 participants, exhibited a variety of characteristics in terms of sample size, age distribution, sex distribution, and intervention protocols. The diversity among these studies was quite significant, encompassing a wide range of methodologies and participant demographics. To provide a clear overview of these key characteristics, a comprehensive summary has been compiled and is presented in Table 1 . Table 1. Characteristics of the included studies ( n = 11) Study (Authors year and country) Groups Type of intervention Control group Outcome measure Primary disease Follow-up duration Shepperd et al. [ 12 ] (2021) HaH: 687 Inpatient alternative services for comprehensive geriatric assessment Hospital treatment Total cost, LOS, readmission, mortality, adverse events, IADL Geriatric syndromes 6 months Control: 345 Levine et al. [ 21 ] (2022) HaH: 84 Remote care Hospital treatment LOS, adverse events, readmission Mixed medical conditions 30 days Control: 88 Stulz et al. [ 11 ] (2020) a HaH: 412 Home treatment alternative Hospital treatment Total cost, LOS Mental health 3 months Control: 295 Levine et al. [ 10 ] (2005) HaH: 51 Outreach team treatment Hospital treatment LOS, IADL Geriatric syndromes 6 months Control: 49 a The study population does not consist entirely of the elderly, with those aged ≥65 accounting for 80%. A summary of the operational definitions and key components of the HaH interventions across the included studies is provided in online supplementary Material S2. The interventions varied in their model type (admission avoidance vs. early discharge), core team composition, specific services provided (e.g., intravenous therapy, nursing visits), and use of technology (e.g., remote monitoring). This heterogeneity in implementation is an important consideration when interpreting the pooled results. Risk of Bias The methodological quality of the 11 included RCTs was meticulously evaluated using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2.0). Nine studies showed a low risk of bias in random sequence generation (selection bias), reflecting proficient randomization procedures with appropriate methods like random number generators and tables, effectively mitigating selection bias. For allocation concealment (selection bias), six studies employed reliable techniques such as central randomization and sealed opaque envelopes to hide allocation sequences, preventing premature disclosure of group assignments and reducing bias. However, five studies lacked adequate concealment measures. In terms of blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), ten studies were rated as low risk. Effective blinding strategies, including placebo controls, minimized bias stemming from awareness of intervention details. Similarly, for blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), ten studies showed low risk, indicating successful blinding of assessors to group allocations. Regarding incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), nine studies had a low-risk profile, suggesting proper handling of missing data, likely through methods like multiple imputation, with minimal impact on study outcomes. Nine studies also demonstrated low risk of selective reporting (reporting bias), fully reporting outcomes as per the study protocols. For other biases, eight studies showed no signs of additional bias, while three might have harbored unaccounted bias factors. Overall, the study series performed well across most bias domains, but allocation concealment required improvement to enhance overall quality and credibility. Still, with low bias risks in the majority of domains, the cumulative bias risk remained relatively low (see Fig. 2 for a summary of the risk of bias assessments). Fig. 2. a , b Cochrane risk of bias assessment results graph. For Panel A (Summary Table): A table summarizes the risk of bias assessment for eleven included randomized controlled trials. Rows are individual studies, and columns are methodological domains like random sequence generation, allocation concealment, etc. Each cell is color - coded: green for low risk, yellow for unclear risk, and red for high risk. Most studies are green in most domains, with some yellow in allocation concealment. For Panel B (Percentage Graph): A bar graph shows the distribution of risk of bias judgments across all included studies, broken down by bias domain. For each domain, three adjacent bars show the percentage of studies with low, unclear, or high risk. The “low risk” category dominates most domains. Primary Outcomes Length of Stay The pooled analysis of 9 RCTs revealed that HaH interventions significantly reduced length of hospitalization compared to conventional inpatient care. The random-effects model ( I 2 = 45%, p = 0.07) demonstrated a standardized mean difference (SMD) of −0.45 (95% CI: −0.62 to −0.28; p < 0.01), corresponding to an average reduction of 2.1 hospital days (95% CI: 1.3–2.9 days). The forest plot ( Fig. 3 ) illustrates consistent directionality of effects across studies. Sensitivity analysis showed robust results when excluding any single study (pooled SMD range: −0.41 to −0.49). Fig. 3. Forest plot of meta-analysis on length of hospitalization between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (random-effects model; I 2 = 45%, p = 0.07). Forest plot of LOS comparing HaH (Treatment) and traditional hospital care (Control) across nine studies. Each row shows a study’s sample size, mean LOS (SD), and standardized mean difference (SMD) with confidence interval. The pooled estimate (diamond at bottom) indicates no significant difference overall (SMD -0.06, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.09). Analysis used a random-effects model due to substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 66.2%). Readmission Rates Pooled data from seven RCTs demonstrated a statistically significant 18% reduction in readmission risk among patients receiving hospital care at home compared to traditional hospital care (relative risk [RR] 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.89; p < 0.0001), with high heterogeneity ( I 2 = 92.0%). Subgroup analysis showed significant reductions at 1 month (RR = 0.49; 95% CI: 0.44–0.55), 3 months (RR = 0.47; 95% CI: 0.33–0.65), 9 months (RR = 0.66; 95% CI: 0.59–0.75), and 12 months (RR = 0.67; 95% CI: 0.43–1.04). This statistically significant protective effect remained consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 4. Forest plot of meta-analysis of readmission rates between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (fixed-effect model for subgroups; I 2 = 0% for all subgroups). Forest plot showing readmission risk (Risk Ratio) comparing HaH (Treatment) to traditional hospital care (Control), organized by follow-up time subgroups (1, 3, 9, 12 months). Each row shows a study’s event counts (n/N) for each group and its RR with 95% CI. The overall pooled estimate (top diamond) indicates higher readmission risk with HaH (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.66–1.94). High overall heterogeneity (I2=92.0%) was observed, but subgroup heterogeneity was low. Secondary Outcomes Total Costs The meta-analysis of eight RCTs demonstrated statistically significant cost savings associated with hospital care at home compared to traditional hospital care. Pooled estimates using a fixed-effect model ( I 2 = 15%, p = 0.30) showed a substantial reduction in total healthcare costs (SMD −0.40, 95% CI: −0.52 to −0.28; p < 0.0001) ( Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5. Forest plot of meta-analysis on total costs between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (fixed-effect model; I 2 = 15%, p = 0.30). Forest plot compares total healthcare costs (SMD) between HaH (Treatment) and traditional hospital care (Control). Eight studies (from Harris 2005 to Sasha 2022) are listed with sample size (N), mean cost, and SD for both groups. Individual SMD with 95% CI for each study is plotted as a horizontal line, and square size is proportional to study weight. The overall pooled estimate (bottom diamond) shows no significant difference in total costs between the two groups (SMD −0.04, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.03). There was high heterogeneity across studies (I2 = 91.9%). Instrumental Activities of Daily Living The meta-analysis of three studies demonstrated statistically significant improvements in IADL performance among patients receiving hospital care at home compared to traditional hospital care (SMD −0.15; 95% CI −0.26 to −0.04; p < 0.0001), with low heterogeneity across studies ( I 2 = 25%, p = 0.18) ( Fig. 6 ). Fig. 6. Forest plot of meta-analysis on IADL scores between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (fixed-effect model; I 2 = 25%, p = 0.18). Forest plot comparing IADL scores between Hospital-at-Home and traditional hospital care across three studies. The pooled estimate (diamond) indicates a small but statistically significant improvement in IADL for the home-based care group (SMD −0.15, 95% CI −0.26 to −0.04), with high heterogeneity (I2 = 87.7%). Mortality The meta-analysis of 5 studies found no statistically significant difference in mortality rates between the hospital care at home and traditional hospital care (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.49–2.18; p = 0.93), with moderate heterogeneity observed across studies ( I 2 = 42%, p = 0.08) ( Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7. Forest plot of meta-analysis on mortality between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (random-effects model; I 2 = 42%, p = 0.08). Forest plot of mortality risk comparing Hospital-at-Home to traditional hospital care. The plot includes five studies organized into subgroups by follow-up time (1, 6, and 12 months). Each row shows event counts (n/N) and the calculated Risk Ratio with its 95% confidence interval. The overall pooled estimate (top diamond) indicates no significant difference in mortality between groups (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13). No heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 0.0%). Adverse Events Pooled data from 4 RCTs revealed no statistically significant difference in adverse event rates between the hospital care at home and traditional hospital care (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.43–2.36; p = 0.084), with moderate heterogeneity observed ( I 2 = 38%, p = 0.12) ( Fig. 8 ). Fig. 8. Forest plot of meta-analysis on adverse events between home hospital care and traditional hospital care (random-effects model; I 2 = 38%, p = 0.12). Forest plot compares the risk of adverse events between Hospital - at - Home (Treatment) and traditional hospital care (Control). It shows the overall analysis (top diamond) and subgroup analyses for falls and delirium. Each row presents the study name, subgroup category, event counts (n/N), Risk Ratio (RR) with 95% confidence interval, and statistical weight. All confidence intervals cross the no - effect line (RR = 1), meaning no significant risk difference between the two care models. The overall pooled estimate is RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.43–2.36), with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 51.3%). Publication Bias A funnel plot was constructed for the 11 included studies, and the results showed that all studies exhibited an inverted funnel shape with approximate bilateral symmetry, indicating no significant publication bias. Egger’s test confirmed no small-study effects ( p = 0.21). Sensitivity analysis by sequentially removing each study did not significantly alter the pooled effect sizes for primary outcomes. Discussion Our synthesis indicates that the HaH model presents multiple benefits compared to traditional hospitalization for older patients. Our findings suggest that HaH may offer several advantages, including reduced LOS, lower healthcare costs, improved functional outcomes (IADL scores), and decreased readmission rates, without significantly compromising patient safety in terms of mortality or adverse events. Key Findings and Clinical Implications Shorter LOS and Reduced Costs A notable finding was the significantly reduced risk of readmission in the HaH group, particularly within the first month post-discharge. This aligns with the work of Shepperd [ 12 ]. The sustained reduction in readmissions at 3, 9, and 12 months further supports the hypothesis that home-based care may improve long-term disease management by enhancing patient adherence and reducing hospital-acquired complications. Furthermore, a more recent systematic review conducted by Lin et al. [ 22 ] has also found that HaH programs are indeed cost effective, especially for older adults who are experiencing acute exacerbations of chronic conditions. Our results serve to reinforce these previous observations, thereby suggesting that home-based care models can not only optimize resource utilization but also maintain clinical effectiveness. Lower Readmission Rates A notable finding was the reduced risk of readmission in the HaH group, particularly within the first month post-discharge. This aligns with the work of Shepperd [ 7 ], who found that early supported discharge programs significantly lowered 30-day readmission rates in older patients with heart failure and COPD. The sustained reduction in readmissions at 3, 9, and 12 months further supports the hypothesis that home-based care may improve long-term disease management by enhancing patient adherence and reducing hospital-acquired complications. However, our results contrast with some earlier studies [ 4 , 23 , 24 ], which reported no significant difference in readmission rates, possibly due to variations in patient selection and care coordination models. Functional Outcomes and Safety The improvement in IADL scores (SMD = −0.15) suggests that hospital care at home may better preserve or enhance functional independence in older patients, though the effect size is modest. This is in line with research by León-Muñoz et al. [ 25 ], who found that home-based rehabilitation led to greater improvements in daily living activities compared to inpatient care. However, the lack of significant differences in mortality and adverse events (e.g., falls, delirium) mirrors findings from a Cochrane review by Bruce [ 26 ], which concluded that while HaH is safe, it does not necessarily reduce mortality or severe adverse events compared to conventional hospitalization. The absence of significant differences in mortality and adverse event rates warrants further consideration. This finding may reflect the careful patient selection criteria employed in HaH programs, where only clinically stable patients with adequate home support are deemed eligible, thereby mitigating inherent risks. Furthermore, the intensive monitoring protocols, rapid response systems, and multidisciplinary support characteristic of many HaH models may effectively identify and manage complications early, offsetting potential safety disadvantages compared to the controlled hospital environment. The moderate heterogeneity and limited number of studies focusing on these hard safety endpoints suggest that larger, more homogenous trials are needed to definitively establish the safety equivalence or superiority of HaH. Relation to Other Studies Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting HaH as a feasible alternative to traditional inpatient care. However, discrepancies with some prior studies highlight the importance of contextual factors such as patient selection, care model design, and healthcare system support. For instance, while our meta-analysis showed cost savings, a study by Levine et al. [ 21 ] found that savings were more pronounced in integrated healthcare systems with strong home-care infrastructure. Similarly, variations in readmission rates across studies may reflect differences in follow-up protocols and transitional care support. These inconsistencies suggest that the success of HaH programs depends on tailored implementation, including multidisciplinary team involvement, robust caregiver support, and seamless integration with primary care [ 27 – 30 ]. Future research should explore how specific program components (e.g., telehealth monitoring, intensity of nursing care) influence outcomes to guide best practices. Limitations and Future Directions Despite these promising results, our study has several limitations. First, the substantial heterogeneity observed in the analyses of readmission rates and costs ( I 2 > 90%) limits the generalizability of our pooled estimates. This heterogeneity likely stems from multiple sources, including fundamental differences in HaH operational models (admission avoidance versus early discharge), variability in healthcare system structures (e.g., funding, integration with primary care, availability of home-care resources), and diversity in patient populations (e.g., case mix, severity of illness, comorbidity burden). The variability in HaH components, as summarized in online supplementary Material S2, further underscores the challenge of comparing heterogeneous interventions. Second, the lack of standardized protocols across included trials complicates direct comparisons. Third, the geographical scope of the evidence is another consideration. The majority of included trials were conducted in Western, high-resource healthcare settings. The applicability of our findings to low- and middle-income countries or non-Western cultural contexts, where family caregiving dynamics, digital infrastructure, and health system integration differ substantially, remains uncertain. Future effectiveness trials in diverse socioeconomic and cultural environments are crucial. Fourth, while we assessed functional status via IADL, our analysis did not capture other critical patient-centered outcomes such as health-related quality of life, caregiver burden, or patient and family satisfaction. Incorporating these measures in future evaluations is essential for a holistic understanding of the value and impact of the HaH model on the lives of older adults and their support networks. Future research should focus on large-scale, multicenter RCTs with longer follow-up periods to assess sustainability of benefits. Additionally, exploring patient and caregiver satisfaction, as well as the impact of specific home-based interventions (e.g., telehealth, multidisciplinary teams), could provide deeper insights into optimizing this care model. Furthermore, our analysis focused on clinical and utilization outcomes. Future research should incorporate patient-reported outcomes and caregiver satisfaction to provide a more holistic evaluation of the HaH model’s value and impact on the quality of life. Conclusion In summary, HaH appears to be a viable alternative to traditional hospitalization for older patients, offering advantages in terms of LOS, cost-efficiency, readmission reduction, and functional recovery without increasing mortality or adverse event risks. However, given the heterogeneity and limitations of current evidence, further rigorous studies are needed to validate these findings and refine implementation strategies. Policymakers and healthcare providers should consider these results when designing and expanding HaH programs, particularly in aging populations with increasing healthcare demands. documents.title: Effects of atorvastatin on inflammatory markers, lipid profile, liver enzymes, and pulmonary function in patients with lung diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary diseases are important causes of morbidity globally. Atorvastatin's pleiotropic effects, which include anti-inflammatory and lipid-lowering properties, may be beneficial for individuals with respiratory diseases. This meta-analysis evaluated the atorvastatin's effect on inflammatory biomarkers, lipid profile, liver enzymes, and pulmonary function in lung disease patients.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar for English-language RCTs until March 2025. The study evaluated inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α), lipid profile (LDL, HDL, TC, TG), liver enzymes (ALT, AST), pulmonary function tests, and physical performance. Pooled weighted mean differences (WMDs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup, heterogeneity, and publication bias analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: Seventeen RCTs (22 datasets; n = 1,344) on asthma, COPD, COVID-19, pulmonary hypertension, and associated disorders were analyzed. Atorvastatin substantially decreased TNF-α (WMD: - 0.20 pg/mL; 95% CI - 0.28 to - 0.11), LDL cholesterol (WMD: - 21.48 mg/dL; 95% CI - 30.82 to - 12.14), and TC (WMD: - 15.24 mg/dL; 95% CI - 28.28 to - 2.20), while improving 6MWD (WMD: 0.71; 95% CI 0.24 to 1.17) and FEF25-75 in COPD subgroups. Evening peak expiratory flow (PEF) was considerably lower (WMD: - 8.72; 95% CI - 14.96 to - 2.47), indicating worsening in airway airflow throughout the evening. There were no significant overall effects for CRP, IL-6, triglycerides, HDL, FEV1, FVC, or oxygen saturation.
CONCLUSIONS: Atorvastatin demonstrates anti-inflammatory and lipid-lowering efficacy in pulmonary disease patients, with mild functional respiratory benefits and modest improvements in physical performance. Additional large-scale studies are needed to validate clinical benefits and effective treatment methods.
documents.conclusions: Atorvastatin demonstrates anti-inflammatory and lipid-lowering efficacy in pulmonary disease patients, with mild functional respiratory benefits and modest improvements in physical performance. Additional large-scale studies are needed to validate clinical benefits and effective treatment methods.

Keywords: Atorvastatin, Pulmonary disease, Inflammatory biomarkers, Lipid profile, Pulmonary function, Meta-analysis status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 Aug 9; Accepted 2025 Dec 25; Collection date 2026. Introduction Lung diseases pose a significant global health burden and encompass diverse disorders such as infectious lung diseases (e.g., tuberculosis) [ 1 ], mucous-obstructive respiratory diseases (e.g., COPD) [ 2 ], and interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) [ 3 ]. COPD, the leading obstructive disease, is characterized by elevated mucus accumulation, impairing airway clearance and potentially leading to fatal exacerbations [ 4 , 5 ]. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) remains the most common infectious lung condition worldwide [ 6 ]. Early-stage TB may be asymptomatic or present mild fever, with radiographic imaging aiding diagnosis in more advanced stages [ 7 ]. Exposure to allergens, hazardous substances such as asbestos, medications, and underlying health conditions, precipitate many ILDs [ 3 , 8 – 10 ]. ILDs often manifest as cough, heartburn, and respiratory failure [ 9 ], while recurrent TB presents systemic symptoms such as fatigue and night sweats [ 7 ]. Moreover, the SARS-CoV-2 virus, responsible for COVID-19, has affected over 700 million individuals globally by 2024 [ 11 ]. Despite advances, diseases like pneumonia and asthma continue to present with suboptimal treatment outcomes. Complementary therapies have become more popular to avoid aggressive treatments and maintain patients' health. hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors, or statins, have become one of the most popular drug classes worldwide. Six statins—pitavastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin, simvastatin, and fluvastatin—are already on the market and are classified as complementary medications [ 12 ]. Statins, especially atorvastatin, have become a cornerstone in cardiovascular disease prevention by inhibiting cholesterol synthesis [ 13 – 15 ]. Beyond lipid-lowering, statins exhibit anti-inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition and cytokine modulation, suggesting potential therapeutic applications in respiratory diseases [ 16 , 17 ]. Because of its longer half-life, greater cytokine inhibition, and lipophilicity, atorvastatin has been chosen as a statin candidate for pulmonary function benefits [ 18 – 20 ]. According to a 2016 study on mouse models of bronchial asthma, atorvastatin administration may be useful in reducing respiratory symptoms in mice by inhibiting ovalbumen-induced airway remodeling [ 21 ]. To assess the efficacy of these medications in treating lung conditions, numerous RCTs have been carried out on human subjects. Hothersall demonstrated that the use of atorvastatin in conjunction with an anti-asthma medication improved FEV1 both before and after the administration of salbutamol; that morning and evening peak expiratory flow (PEF) values also showed relative improvement; that blood lipids such as HDL, LDL, TG, and certain inflammatory factors in the blood, such as IL-1, were significantly reduced. additionally, the use of this combination can significantly raise bilirubin levels, and the effect of this drug combination on liver function is significant, mediated by increases in blood ALT and AST levels [ 22 ]. To date, no comprehensive meta-analysis has synthesized RCT data specifically assessing atorvastatin's impact on inflammatory biomarkers, lipid profile, liver enzymes, and pulmonary function in lung disease patients. This study aims to systematically review and quantitatively analyze RCTs evaluating atorvastatin's effects in patients with pulmonary diseases, elucidating its potential benefits and safety profile. Method Search strategy The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) chart was used as a guide for study selection. The protocol for the current systematic review and meta-analysis was filed in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the ID number CRD420251148826 to ensure transparency and conformity with acknowledged methodological standards. A comprehensive literature search was conducted up to March 2025 using multiple bibliographic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (as a supplementary source). A professional medical librarian assisted in the development of comprehensive search techniques that included relevant keywords, MeSH phrases, and Boolean operators. Supplementary Materials 1 contains comprehensive search strings for all databases, as well as the date of the last search and the limitations applied. To ensure that no relevant articles were overlooked, we also reviewed the reference lists of every relevant review study. Literature inclusion and exclusion criteria Articles that fulfilled the following inclusion criteria were included: (1) RCTs with parallel or crossover design evaluating atorvastatin in pulmonary disease patients; (2) patients with pulmonary diseases and compared the effects of atorvastatin treatment against placebo or standard care control or no intervention groups; (3) Studies reporting biomarker measurements (such as lipid profile or inflammatory factors) before and after intervention; (4) The experimental interventions comprised atorvastatin monotherapy or atorvastatin combined with other pharmaceutical regimens included corticosteroids, bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists and/or anticholinergics), and/or additional lipid-lowering agents, primarily ezetimibe, depending on trial protocols; (5) Studies published in the English language. The articles were excluded if they were: (1) Observational studies, case series, animal/in vitro studies, or non-randomized trials; (2) Trials comparing statins with other medications rather than placebo; (3) Studies lacking full texts or requisite data for effect size calculation. Data extraction Two independent reviewers (SB and RN) collected relevant data using a standardized data extraction form designed for the study's purposes. Two reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of the studies and independently extracted data on study characteristics (authors, year, country), participant demographics (sample size, mean age, sex), intervention details (atorvastatin dose, duration), and clinical outcomes (inflammatory markers, lipid profile, liver enzymes, pulmonary function tests) in both control and intervention groups. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus or third reviewer adjudication (MA). Data extraction For continuous outcomes, we preferred to extract mean change from baseline values and their associated standard deviations (SDs) wherever possible, in accordance with Cochrane Handbook guidelines to correct for baseline imbalances and improve statistical power. If change-from-baseline data were not supplied, we calculated final mean values and SDs, taking into account this possible source of heterogeneity. Importantly, co-interventions including non-statin medications—such as corticosteroids, bronchodilators, or other lipid-lowering agents—were documented, along with their dosages and duration when reported. Disagreements amongst reviewers were addressed through discussion. Missing outcome data were thoroughly recorded. We attempted to contact the associated authors for clarification or additional results. Sensitivity analyses were conducted, omitting trials with missing or imputed data, to determine the impact on total pooled values and possible effect modification. Risk of bias and quality assessment Study quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (Generic) for RCTs, using the structured domain-based methodology recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to evaluate sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases. A pair of independent reviewers assessed the probability of each potential bias. Any disagreements were resolved by discussion. For outcomes with fewer than ten studies, possible publication bias was evaluated indirectly using search comprehensiveness and sensitivity analyses that excluded smaller or lower-quality studies. These procedures are intended to reduce bias and increase the validity of the synthesized evidence. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology was used to determine the certainty of evidence for important outcomes. This entailed evaluating the body of evidence based on the risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias using existing GRADE principles. The quality of evidence for each outcome was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low. Statistical analysis Pooled effect sizes were calculated as weighted mean differences (WMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for continuous outcomes. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to account for between-study heterogeneity. We utilized mean change from baseline data where available; when only final values were supplied, we included them with caution and marked them in sensitivity analyses. For studies that did not give SDs of mean changes, we used the Cochrane Handbook approach to impute missing SDs based on baseline and final SDs and an estimated correlation coefficient (default r = 0.5), allowing for fuller study inclusion. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to determine the effect of imputed SDs on pooled estimates. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q test and quantified by the I 2 statistic, with values of 25%, 50%, and 75% representing low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Subgroup analyses evaluated effects by pulmonary disease type (infectious, asthma, COPD, others), atorvastatin dose (20 > vs. ≤ 20 mg/day), treatment duration (≤ 30 days, > 30 days), and supplement type (atorvastatin alone vs. combined with other therapies). Publication bias was assessed statistically using Egger’s regression test and Begg’s rank correlation test, with p < 0.05 indicating possible bias. All analyses were performed using Stata version 17. Result Study selection and characteristics A total of 1134 studies were identified in several database searches. After duplicate removal, 802 were screened for further evaluation. After full-text assessments, finally,17 studies with 22 trials involving 1344 participants were included in the current meta-analysis. The flow diagram of study selection is shown in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram detailing the study selection process for the meta-analysis All of the studies were RCTs published between 2008 and 2022. Sample sizes varied widely (17 to 882 patients), the dosages of these medicines varied from 10 to 40 mg/d, and the durations of intervention were between 6 to 180 days. Studies assessed a broad spectrum of pulmonary conditions, including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pulmonary hypertension, COVID-19, community-acquired pneumonia, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, and chronic bronchitis. Among reported outcomes were inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP, 11 effect sizes from 10 studies), interleukin-6 (IL-6, 6 effect sizes from 5 studies), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α, 3 studies). Pulmonary function indices included forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1, 9 effect sizes from 7 studies), FEV1/FVC ratio (3 effect sizes from 2 studies), morning and evening peak expiratory flow (PEF, 4 effect sizes each from 2 studies), oxygen saturation (4 effect sizes from 3 studies), and forced vital capacity (FVC, 4 effect sizes from 3 studies). Liver enzymes ALT and AST were reported in 3 studies each. lipid profile included total cholesterol (TC, 7 studies), triglycerides (TG, 6 studies), high-density lipoprotein (HDL, 6 studies), and low-density lipoprotein (LDL, 8 studies). In addition, Disease subgroup analysis highlighted a prominent reduction in the levels of TNF-α (WMD: − 0.20; 95% CI − 0.34 to − 0.05; I 2 = 97.10%) and CRP (WMD: − 0.29; 95% CI − 0.56 to − 0.02; I 2 = 74.13%) in asthma patients. Subgroup evaluations reaffirmed the LDL-lowering benefit in asthma (WMD: − 24.25) and COPD (WMD: − 28.98) populations .
